articles.title: Israeli raids and arrests in southern Syria push population to the brink
articles.summary: Survivors recount brutal prison conditions, enduring beatings, restraints and psychological abuse by Israeli soldiers.
articles.body:
Qatana, Syria – In the living room of his home, Ahmed explains in a low voice how he was beaten and tortured in an Israeli prison after he was arrested at a checkpoint the Israeli military had set up on the street in his village in Syria.

“They stopped me, they asked for my name, asked where I’m from,” he says. “I gave my name and village. They said, ‘You need to come with us for five minutes, and we’ll bring you back.'”

He says he then spent more than one year detained in Israel. For 90 days, he was in handcuffs and describes being thrown to the cell floor, beaten with sticks while restrained with his hands behind his back.

“They tighten the cuffs by stamping on them with their feet, until the cuffs bite into the flesh of your wrists and also your buttocks. Sometimes they leave them tightened like this for one or two days until your hands are extremely swollen. Your hands go green, and you can’t feel them at all.”

After his release this month, dozens of people gathered outside his home to congratulate him on his return, and to seek any scrap of information about their own relatives who are still missing. Al Jazeera has ascertained that there are at least 51 Syrians still detained inside Israel. Many were held in the notorious Sde Teiman military prison , but have since been transferred to facilities run by the Israel Prison Service. Al Jazeera has confirmed Syrians have been moved to Ofer, al-Jalama (Kishon) and Megiddo. A small number have been released.

The impact is ongoing. Mahmoud – a pseudonym – had been home for nine days when Al Jazeera interviewed him. “Until now I feel unstable; I’m not normal. I feel crazy sometimes in the night. I go to look at my kids because I can’t believe I’m really home.”

Mahmoud pauses as his six-year-old son carries in a tray of wobbling tea glasses and sets it carefully on the carpeted floor. The glasses clink, and the window shakes. The children turn their heads towards the sound of artillery. Since early August, the Israeli military has fired shells into the fields most days, preventing farmers and shepherds from working, occasionally killing livestock and regularly terrifying the population. In September, the Sijil Center, a Syrian organisation that monitors Israeli activity, documented 280 Israeli violations of the 1974 agreement between the two countries, including incursions, raids and arrests, as well as artillery and machine-gun fire.

UN forces have patrolled a demilitarised zone between the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights and the rest of Syria since the 1974 agreement, but Israel occupied more Syrian land in the immediate aftermath of the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime in December 2024. The peacekeepers remain, but have limited capacity to restrain Israeli military activity, which continues to increase .

In one incident in late August, two Israeli tanks and five other armoured vehicles descended from one of their hilltop bases and blocked the only access road to United Nations Disengagement Observer Force base 37, near the village of Jubata al-Khashab. A man who works for the local council called the UN base, which houses a peacekeeping mission established in 1974 to maintain the Israeli-Syrian ceasefire, and asked if they needed assistance.

“I think they were offended,” he laughed. “And they told me ‘, No, stay where you are; don’t you or anybody else come down here. We’ll call for help from another base if we need it.'”

UNDOF confirmed to Al Jazeera that the movement of their personnel continues to be “restricted on occasion” by the Israeli military, and that Israel’s practice of setting up roadblocks and checkpoints is “preventing UNDOF from conducting its planned and mandated patrol activities”.

Residents sometimes seek help from peacekeepers when people are detained at checkpoints, but there is little they can do about the midnight raids.

Mahmoud was detained at 3:30am when Israeli troops surrounded his home, calling for him by name and brandishing a photo of him from social media. Nine days after his release, he crouches, kneeling and pressing his forehead to the ground with his hands behind his head.

“They make us sit like this for hours,” he says, noting that he ended up with infected wounds on his knees from the cell floor. He has scars on his wrists and ankles from being restrained.

“They cuff you so you can’t move and then release the dogs,” he says. “They have muzzles on, but they ran into us, like a body slam.” The metal muzzles, he explains, made the impact stronger and caused bleeding.

“I want to tell you about the ‘disco room’,” he says. “It’s a room full of speakers; they put detainees in there, and the music is very loud.” He described seeing Syrian, Palestinian and Lebanese prisoners throwing up when they were allowed out.

Mahmoud was never charged, and says he does not know why he was released. He says that he was never granted access to a lawyer throughout his detention. The Red Cross has been denied access to detainees in Israeli detention since October 7, 2023, the date of the Hamas-led attack on Israel and the start of Israel’s subsequent genocidal war on Gaza.

“They make sure you understand the moment you enter that you are stripped of all your rights; they tell you this explicitly.”

Al Jazeera has contacted the Israeli military for comment, but has yet to receive a response. Israel says that its occupation of Syrian land and incursions deeper into Syria are necessary for security reasons, and to defend Syria’s Druze community, which it says is threatened by the authorities in Syria – a claim the Syrian government rejects.

Ahmed was bewildered by this treatment. He told Al Jazeera that he was not even questioned until nearly five months into his detention. He was asked whether he, or anyone he knew, was a member of Hezbollah, Hamas, ISIL (ISIS) or a list of other armed groups which had little in common and fought on opposite sides during the war in Syria.

Mohammed Seyyed was detained in 2025. Israeli troops had conducted an incursion the previous day, wreaking destruction on his home and farm. He, his son, his brother and his nephew had gone to make repairs when they were detained and taken into Israel. He was brought to the interrogation room bound and blindfolded. When an Israeli officer freed his eyes, they showed him maps and photographs of his home and neighbourhood.

“Even the barber who cuts my hair, they knew his name, his address,” he said. “They were letting me know they knew everything about me. That any question they might ask, they already knew the answer and would know if I was lying.”

But when the questions came, they were general. The Israeli officers seemed to know everything about him, except what he was accused of. Mohammed told Al Jazeera that one of the officers admitted he had been detained based on false information, which he attributed to reports made by those in his community who inform for Israel.

The fallout of Israeli military activity is wide-ranging. Impromptu checkpoints mean many residents are afraid to leave their homes. Road closures have an impact long after the Israeli soldiers leave: students who need to travel for university consider relocating to Damascus to guarantee they can attend classes, and people with health conditions worry about being blocked from reaching care.

The Syrian government is in a difficult position; Israel has blocked its forces from operating in the south, and it doesn’t have the military strength to confront its neighbour even if the authorities wished to. Instead, they have been attempting to negotiate a security agreement, but talks have largely stalled since the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran.

Residents are losing patience and have begun to protest. In Qatana, local sheikhs gathered after Friday prayers.

“They tested our patience in Daraa,” said Sheikh Mamdouh Tahhan, referring to an incident in Abidin where locals confronted Israeli troops. “As a state we don’t have the ability to get into a war with Israel, but as people we are ready.”

The families of some of those detained feel abandoned by their government. They complain about the lack of legal or financial assistance, noting that with their breadwinners missing, they have run up debts worth hundreds of dollars at local grocery stores.

The families have created a WhatsApp group to exchange news and information, sometimes looking for signs in a sky that is heavy with the sound of Israeli warplanes flying low, and the persistent buzz of a surveillance drone. “From the morning I’ve been listening, and I’ve been hearing the drone,” one mother says. “I have a hunch that because the drone is up, maybe there will be a release today.”

For several weeks in a row, people were released on Wednesdays. It has become a day of pained anticipation. Hassan Ahmed’s son, then 16, was taken into Israel in April 2025. Israeli troops razed his 400 olive trees shortly after. He has become pivotal in organising protests and hunting for information along with the other parents – in October, Israeli forces raided his farm again, destroying solar panels. Sitting on his balcony, the late afternoon sun filtering through the leaves of a walnut tree, he plays voice notes from other parents that land every minute or so.

“Since this morning, any message that pings on the phone, any new notification I check, hoping somebody has been released,” another mother explains. “Our hearts are on fire. We’re waiting.”

“I’m full of grief,” Hassan says, putting the phone down. “I’ll never be able to describe the pain, it’s very tough. Even trying to describe it makes my heart tighten. I feel like my heart will stop. I feel I will explode.”

articles.title: Black objects, no radar trace: British jets report near-misses with mystery objects amid Russian spy fears
articles.summary: Two RAF jets reported near-misses with unidentified objects flying at up to 17,000 feet over the North Sea, with neither object detected on radar,
articles.body: Two RAF jets reported near-misses with unidentified objects flying at up to 17,000 feet over the North Sea, with neither object detected on radar, according to incident reports reviewed by The Telegraph.According to The Telegraph, an RAF Voyager tanker encountered the first unidentified object on February 18 while refuelling a Typhoon fighter jet off Cromer, Norfolk, at an altitude of 17,000 feet. The pilot reported that the object passed approximately 100 to 150 feet above the tanker.The Voyager's pilot told the RAF radar controller that the small, black object had travelled east to west directly overhead. The controller said he could not see it on radar. In a subsequent report, the pilot said the object's proximity had made him instinctively duck.The second incident occurred on February 23, when an RAF Typhoon pilot spotted a black, circular object, described as similar in size to a car tyre, passing approximately 300 feet above his aircraft during simulated dogfight training off Humberside, at around 12,000 to 12,500 feet.The Typhoon pilot reported the sighting to the radar controller, who subsequently referred the incident to North Yorkshire Police. The incident report said the object was not detected on radar, while the RAF concluded that the pilots had acted appropriately.The first object’s reported altitude was 17,000 feet, 42.5 times the usual 400-foot height limit for civilian drones in the UK. However, the Voyager pilot later said he could not positively identify the object as a drone and acknowledged it could have been a balloon or something similar.Russia suspected of using shadow fleet for drone surveillanceThe sightings come amid allegations that Russia has used its so-called shadow fleet of oil tankers to support drone surveillance operations across Europe.A report by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), published in July 2026, assessed that the Kremlin had very likely conducted a coordinated drone campaign across European countries between August 2024 and February 2026, with Russian-linked vessels likely serving as launch and recovery platforms.The IISS report examined 144 suspected drone incidents across 13 Nato countries and Ireland, including sightings near military installations and critical infrastructure. It said the suspected campaign could have been aimed at gathering intelligence, testing air defence responses and identifying vulnerabilities around sensitive sites.The report also linked suspected drone activity near British military installations, including RAF Lakenheath and RAF Fairford, to the broader pattern of surveillance incidents across Europe.

articles.title: Canada’s Mark Carney makes final appeal against Alberta separation ahead of referendum
articles.summary: EDMONTON, Alberta — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a final appeal to voters considering a path toward independence in his home province of Alberta on Friday, warning that a referendum is a dangerous gamble at a time of growing threats to Canada’s sovereignty.
articles.body: EDMONTON, Alberta — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a final appeal to voters considering a path toward independence in his home province of Alberta on Friday, warning that a referendum is a dangerous gamble at a time of growing threats to Canada’s sovereignty. With U.S. President Donald Trump waging a trade war and threatening to make Canada the 51st state, Carney warned that the referendum comes at the “worst possible time” and urged Albertans not to take the outcome for granted. “Don’t let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome,” Carney told a pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, where he grew up. “This is not a game. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he said. Monday’s vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, home to most of Canada’s proven oil reserves — the fourth largest in the world — will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. Carney’s closing appeal came after two days of campaigning against separation in the province. Earlier Friday, the Liberal prime minister joined Alberta’s conservative premier Danielle Smith in a show of unity against independence. Smith praised Carney for improving relations with a province that frequently clashed with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, over his carbon tax and other energy policies. “I think what we can agree on is that we have had some real change in the last 18 months,” Smith said alongside Carney in Red Deer, Alberta. Smith noted that Carney grew up in Alberta and remains an Edmonton Oilers fan. “He can’t be all bad, right?” she joked. Trump’s threats raise the stakes “Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us. Never. Never,” Carney warned Friday in Edmonton, repeating a warning he made a day earlier in Calgary. At Thursday’s Calgary rally and Friday’s Edmonton rally, the crowd erupted in its loudest applause when Carney spoke about reducing Canada’s economic dependence on the United States. Carney acknowledged Alberta’s longstanding resentment of federal energy policies. “Growing up, I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” he said. But he also emphasized his deep ties to the province. “Alberta is my home. I grew up here. This city, this province, this country have given me everything: my family, my education, my values,” he said. Some Albertans say the vote shouldn’t have been called Outside the Edmonton rally venue Friday, Alberta independence supporters waved flags and held a sign reading “Say no to Carney’s new world order.” Smith called the referendum despite opposing independence herself. She recently cited a poll showing 22% of Albertans support separation, a figure she said was still too high. Smith also faces pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party. Former Premier Jason Kenney said the independence movement gained influence within the party as activists angry over COVID-19 restrictions, some influenced by conspiracy theories, embraced separatism. But some Albertans who want to remain in Canada are angry with Smith for calling the vote. “I think it’s a travesty really to be putting our province and our country through this when such a small portion of people are rabble rousing and saying they want to separate from Canada,” said Deb Lee, a retired Calgary resident who voted in advance to remain in Canada. Smith said Carney had substantially addressed seven of nine federal laws Alberta opposed. She also cited cooperation on a proposed oil pipeline. Independence advocate Tanya Clemens dismissed the agreements between Carney and Smith as “basically pinky promises” that came with too many conditions. Political leaders unite against separation Carney’s chief political rival, federal Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, also urged Albertans Friday to remain in Canada. “Don’t leave your fellow Canadians behind. Lock arms with them,” Poilievre said. Despite their agreement on keeping Alberta in Canada, Carney and Smith remain divided over nine other questions on Monday’s ballot involving immigration and provincial powers. Smith wants voters to approve them, while Carney has urged their rejection. “For the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together,” Smith said.

articles.title: This song was scientifically designed to soothe babies — and 470 million streams prove it works
articles.summary: Imogen Heap, two scientists and 26 babies made a song. A decade on, it’s still averting meltdowns.
articles.body: As father to both a toddler and an infant, the din of tearful wailing — theirs, not mine (usually) — is the soundtrack to approximately half of all car journeys. I get it. Trapped wind, claustrophobic car seats and long scary tunnels are all legitimate reasons to cry when you’re barely big enough to see out of the window. Like most desperate parents, my wife and I have resorted to jangling keys, scrunching whatever crunchy objects are to hand and offering sing-songy reassurances in unnaturally high-pitched voices. Or, in resignation, we would just mentally tune out until reaching our destination. But then we were introduced to an anti-crying device so powerful that I’ve felt compelled, ever since, to share it with every parent I know. It is a work of both science and sorcery: “The Happy Song.” From the opening outbreak of joyous giggling, its soothing effect on my kids is instantaneous. And this is entirely by design. The two-and-a-half-minute song, which celebrates its 10th anniversary this week, was a collaboration between two psychologists and the Grammy Award-winning (and otherwise very grown-up) musician Imogen Heap. Combining established research on what makes babies happy with the results of infant focus groups, the catchy melody, walking bassline and playful lyrics are almost hypnotic, stopping nascent meltdowns in their tracks. Over the last decade, “The Happy Song” has been streamed over 470 million times on Spotify — more than Marvin Gaye’s “Let’s Get It On” and Simon & Garfunkel’s “Bridge Over Troubled Water.” On YouTube, a continuous 10-hour loop of the song, uploaded by some kind soul, has alone garnered 14 million clicks. “The Happy Song” is now among the biggest royalty-generators for an artist who, in addition to her solo career, comprises one-half of the duo Frou Frou and co-produced Taylor Swift’s “1989.” “I never thought in advance, ‘Oh, this is going to make me loads of money from all the babies in the world,’” she laughed, reflecting on the track’s enduring success, via video call, from her London studio. “I just really wanted to make a song that gave a few minutes’ relief to a family at a point when they’re stuck in a traffic jam or whatever.” A discerning audience “The Happy Song” was commissioned by British baby food brand Cow & Gate, though its corporate origins have largely faded from view. In 2016, the company tasked music psychologist Lauren Stewart (who had previously researched “earworms,” the catchy tunes that get stuck in our heads) and child development psychologist Caspar Addyman (author of “The Laughing Baby”) with producing a happiness-inducing song to give away to parents. They in turn approached Heap, a musician known for embracing technology — and who, at the time, had an 18-month-old child of her own. The pair offered Heap various science-backed recommendations, from using major keys and melodic repetition, to musical devices like drum rolls and rising pitch glides that induce anticipation and surprise. Stewart and Addyman meanwhile surveyed more than 2,000 parents to identify noises their babies responded to, which included animal sounds and other children’s laughter (both of which feature in the song). Their initial brief also suggested singing in “Motherese,” the voice we naturally adopt when talking to babies. “It separates the vowel sounds and makes things a bit easier to follow; it helps babies know that you’re talking to them and not somebody else in the room,” said Addyman, joining the video call with Heap. “And you want to stick to things that babies themselves are capable of pronouncing,” he added. “So ‘plosive’ sounds like ‘pa’ and ‘ba’.” (As opposed to “sonorant” ones, like “la.”) Armed with these recommendations and her own parental instincts (“as a mom,” Heap said, “you just intuitively feel what would be nice, and what felt too trite”), the musician got to work. But the science didn’t stop there. After she composed four different main melodies, the researchers then tested them, at two different speeds, on a focus group of 26 babies aged 6 to 12 months old. Participants’ movements, facial expressions and vocal reactions (along with a little interpretation from accompanying parents) suggested a clear winner. “They really had a strong preference,” said Addyman, reporting that around 80% of the babies preferred the melody that Heap eventually built “The Happy Song” around. Later, more developed iterations of the song were again tested on the babies. In one session, they listened to versions of the song at different tempos and, to Addyman’s surprise, opted for the (slightly) slower one. The researchers had initially suggested that Heap use a fast tempo to reflect infants’ heart rates, which are typically higher than adults’, but the theory clearly had its limits. “There was a fast one and a very fast one,” said Addyman. “I was convinced that faster is always better for babies, but actually it was the not-very-fast one that the babies preferred.” “When you’re making a record, you never get feedback,” added Heap, who welcomed participants’ honest and unadulterated opinions. “Usually, you’re just sitting in the studio going, ‘Is this any good? Is this any good?’ So having these reports come back was just so inspiring and motivating — best audience ever.” Parental approval For all the science involved, serendipity played a part, too. The winning melody was inspired by a ditty sung by Heap’s daughter, Scout. “She gets royalties in other ways,” joked Heap when I ask whether the now-11-year-old gets a share of the spoils. In fact, Scout’s influence is found throughout the song. Lyrical references to a bicycle, submarine, helicopter, choo-choo train, airplane and “rocket to the starrrrs” were inspired by her obsession with transport at the time. Scout also provided the laughter at the start, and was present during Heap’s recording sessions, helping her mother achieve more natural “motherese.” Yet, the magic of “The Happy Song” is not just that kids like it. Unlike the rest of the children’s-music-industrial-complex (looking at you, Cocomelon), I don’t hate it. I find myself humming it on the stairs and while making coffee. It’s an earworm. And while I can’t say I’d listen to “The Happy Song” if I didn’t have kids, I have done so, willingly, hundreds of times. “I’m aware of the songs that drive parents nuts,” Heap said, adding that she wanted to write something that “wasn’t too grating and that had some funny bits.” This is achieved by lyrics that are aimed, partly, at adults. The line most frequently stuck in my head (“I just adore-dore-dore you every day more”) is something that I feel, not them. I don’t care about the wheels on the bus turning, or the inventory of Old MacDonald’s farm, but I do care about loving my kids. “I wanted there to be truth to it, and I wanted it to be fun,” Heap said of the lyrics. This approach also worked for babies, who need not be patronized, Addyman added. “I think the key thing behind the success of ‘The Happy Song’ is that it’s not talking down to them,” he said. Heap said she never really promoted the song, but it has nonetheless been discovered by new generations of parents through word of mouth (or desperation, while frantically searching online for ways to stop a baby crying). When it comes to kids’ songs, parental approval is, perhaps, the most effective marketing tool around. After all, we’re the ones picking the music… for now. In the decade since the song’s release, Heap has been thanked by countless strangers (including me at the start of our interview). Among them were a parent at her daughter’s school who recognized her on account of her voice alone and a dad on an airplane whose baby had been crying non-stop for over an hour. “I was like, ‘Oh my god, oh my god. Do I try it? What do I do?” she recalled thinking on the flight, before — bashfully and apologetically, as she tells it — offering the despairing man the song on a pair of headphones. “I was like, ‘So… shall I play it?’ I played him the song, and the baby heard the laugh at the start and was immediately caught. Just a total change of demeanor. “The dad was almost in tears and just so thankful for this moment to gather himself.”

images.caption: Child development psychologist Caspar Addyman and musician Imogen Heap consult a baby focus group during the creation of "The Happy Song."
Imogen Heap, pictured performing in LA in March 2025.

articles.title: India’s Zorawar light tank faces protection and performance trade-off
articles.summary: India’s Zorawar light tank programme faces a key design challenge as the Army seeks stronger armour protection without compromising the mobility required
articles.body: India’s Zorawar light tank programme faces a key design challenge as the Army seeks stronger armour protection without compromising the mobility required for high-altitude operations along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China. The proposed changes could increase the tank’s weight, require a more powerful engine and affect its induction timeline, with the programme now expected to enter service around 2028-2029, according to reports.Developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Larsen & Toubro (L&T), Zorawar was conceived after the 2020 India-China border confrontation in eastern Ladakh. China’s deployment of Type 15 light tanks highlighted the need for an Indian armoured platform suited to mountainous terrain, where thin air, steep gradients, narrow roads and infrastructure constraints can limit the performance and movement of heavier T-72 and T-90 tanks.The Zorawar was designed around a combat weight of approximately 25 tonnes, allowing it to combine mobility with firepower and be transported by aircraft such as the C-17 Globemaster III. It is powered by a Cummins diesel engine rated at around 760 horsepower and carries a 105mm gun in a Belgian-designed Cockerill 3105 turret.The Army’s reported demand for higher protection would require the tank’s armour to withstand more powerful ammunition. The initial configuration reportedly provides frontal protection to STANAG 4569 Level 4, while the proposed requirements include Level 6 protection against 30mm armour-piercing rounds. Stronger side and rear protection is also under consideration. The challenge is to meet these requirements without significantly reducing the tank’s power-to-weight ratio, acceleration and hill-climbing ability.An option under consideration is modular armour, including bolt-on ceramic protection, this wouldn't require a complete redesign. Adding armour and a hard-kill active protection system could increase the tank’s weight. If the vehicle grows to 30-32 tonnes, its existing engine may no longer deliver the same level of performance, potentially requiring a more powerful powerpack and additional testing.China’s Type 15 offers a reference point. It is heavier, at roughly 33-36 tonnes depending on configuration, and uses a 1,000-horsepower engine, a 105mm gun and modular protection. Its design demonstrates that a heavier platform can operate in high-altitude terrain, but Zorawar’s requirements and logistics are different.The Army plans to acquire 354 light tanks. The first 59 are being developed by DRDO and L&T, while Tata Advanced Systems has emerged as the lowest bidder for the remaining 295, with Mahindra Defence Systems also involved in the competition. A phased approach could allow the initial batch to progress while later vehicles incorporate improved protection. The decision will determine whether Zorawar can improve survivability without losing the mobility that defines its role.

articles.title: Scores detained in Paris as protestors clash with police during nationwide demonstrations in France
articles.summary: More than 100 people have been detained in Paris, as officers deploy tear gas in cities up and down the country. Follow live updates.
articles.body:
• Huge protests : Far-left groups, unions, farmers and Yellow Vest protestors are expected to join students in France today in what could be one of the largest nationwide mobilizations since protests erupted in September. Officers have already deployed tear gas in several cities, including Paris, while around 100 people have been detained.

• Police under scrutiny: Anger among those on the streets has been fueled by tactics deployed by officers in recent weeks, which have resulted in serious injuries.

• Simmering anger: The government has struggled to contain the student protests, which started in support of striking teachers at a suburban high school, before snowballing into a national crisis and attracting global attention, including from President Donald Trump .

More than a half hour before the march was due to start, riot police charged onto the square multiple times under volleys of tear gas.

A student or orchestra was playing as the tear gas was fired, before they were escorted off the square by a human chain to protect them.

The crowd is a real mix of old and young, with placards calling for better returns for taxes and French President Emmanuel Macron’s resignation.

Today’s demonstrations in France are expected to be the biggest yet, with tens of thousands of activists from multiple movements joining an estimated 60 marches, and around 250 planned actions including roadblocks and building blockades, across the country.

Here’s a rundown of who is expected to participate.

Yellow Vests: The gilets jaunes, or Yellow Vests, are part of a grassroots citizens’ movement established in 2018, when more than 250,000 people protested a hike in fuel tax. Named after the yellow high-visibility jackets French motorists must carry in their vehicles, the Yellow Vests are comprised of people from across the political spectrum and have contributed support to a range of protests since they emerged almost a decade ago.

Students: High school students demanding more teachers, reduced class sizes and better building conditions will make up a significant portion of those on the streets. They have been protesting since late September.

Far-left groups: Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise has backed the student movement and is expected to show up at demonstrations in support of the protesters and their demands. The party also described the protests as a potential starting point for a much broader movement, and is demanding a cap on fuel prices.

Farmers: Some farmers have discussed staging tractor protests.

Taxi drivers: Drivers have already begun staging rolling roadblocks and blockades around Paris airports and say they intend to continue through Saturday.

CNN’s Saskya Vandoorne and Catherine Nicholls contributed reporting.

Amid the tens of thousands of protesters expected to take to the streets across France today are the gilets jaunes , or Yellow Vests, part of a grassroots citizens’ movement that began almost a decade ago.

The movement dates back to 2018, when more than 250,000 people protested a rise in fuel tax announced by the government, which it said was to fight against climate change.

The protests – named after the yellow high-visibility jackets French motorists must carry in their vehicles – morphed into broader demonstrations against French President Emmanuel Macron and his government in the weeks following November 2018.

They often turned violent, with at least 10 people dying in connection with the protests in their first six weeks.

The French government made many concessions in the first weeks of the initial Yellow Vest protests, including scrapping the initial fuel tax, and implementing a 10 billion euro ($11.05 billion) package of wage rises and tax relief for the poorest.

The Yellow Vests have taken to the streets several times since those first protests died down. In 2020, police took more than 250 people in for questioning and fired tear gas during violent scenes involving the movement in Paris.

People from across the political spectrum have taken part in Yellow Vest protests, including anarchists, anti-immigration populists and hard-core fascists.

There are even groups on social media claiming to be environmental “yellow jackets,” a direct contradiction of the original protesters’ demands to scrap a new eco-tax.

Some have blamed a radical fringe of the Yellow Vest movement for a rise in anti-semitism in France.

A 2019 study conducted by the Fondation Jean Jaures showed that 50% of those who participated said they believed in a “global Zionist conspiracy.”

CNN’s Melissa Bell, Saskya Vandoorne and Gianluca Mezzofiore contributed to this reporting.

Things have quickly escalated at Paris’ Place de la République, from where today’s main march is expected to begin.

Police have deployed tear gas in the square and charged into the crowd. A small group of protestors have aimed fireworks at police lines.

The square is blocked off on several sides to funnel protestors along the permitted route, although the march is not set to begin for more than an hour.

Police in Lyon launched tear gas grenades to disperse around 300 people who have mobilized outside the city’s Jean Moulin University earlier, according to CNN’s French affiliate BFMTV.

Protests have also begun in Rennes, and in Marseille where officers have also deployed tear gas to disband the crowds.

Around 100 people have already been detained across the Paris region, BFMTV has reported, mostly for the possession of prohibited protective gear.

Hundreds of people have gathered at Paris’ Place de la République, where today’s main march is expected to begin.

Police have fired tear gas towards the crowd, which is currently peaceful.

A smattering of Yellow Vests protesters is also present.

US President Donald Trump joked about “joining the revolution” ahead of the mass protests planned today in Paris, while French President Emanuel Macron called for “calm and respect.”

Speaking from a rally yesterday in Georgia , Trump joked, “Let’s go to France and join the revolution and spend our $5000 there”, touching on the dividend promised if the Republicans win the US midterms.

Last night, speaking from the European council in Brussels , French President Emmanuel Macron asked for “calm” with reference to today’s planned protests.

“There is a constitutional right to protest, but what goes along with this right is respect,” he added.

A challenging summer of heatwaves cast disarray across France’s education system as classrooms without air conditioning became unbearable and examination timetables were disrupted.

This, plus long-standing concerns over inadequate staffing and school conditions, prompted thousands of teenagers to flood the street and demand change.

So, what is it that French students want?

Student union leaders representing the teenaged protesters have urged a €10 billion investment (around $11.2 billion) in high school and university-level education.

Major priorities include more teachers; reduced class sizes and buildings appropriately adapted to withstand climate change, ensuring they remain fit-for-purpose throughout the year.

Students also wish to negotiate their workloads, end a controversial university admissions system, create more student accommodation and end police violence against students.

Protests were initiated after students joined teachers to protest understaffing and a lack of resources at just one school in a Paris suburb on September 21. When demands were met, and extra staff were deployed to the school, demonstrators mobilized throughout Paris and across the country, signaling a nationwide appetite for change.

The government has been criticized as too slow to respond to the requests made by demonstrators, with some suggesting government inaction is emblematic of the students’ frustrations at going unheard, and a reason for their sustained anger.

CNN’s Melissa Bell, Saskya Vandoorne, Lucie Lepellec and Billy Stockwell contributed reporting.

Protests are underway across France this morning, with demonstrations taking place in a number of cities, including Paris and Marseille.

In Marseille, a fire was burning before today’s demonstration began, with one person photographed waving the French flag as they walked by the flames. Meanwhile, in Paris, protestors carried placards, including one reading “What do we want? Resignation.”

Police officers were photographed standing guard near the protests. Take a look at the latest images we’re seeing, below.

Meanwhile, student demonstrations were also held across Italy yesterday to protest against the precarious state of public schools and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s recent cap on foreign students in classrooms.

Several events turned violent, including in Rome, Bologna and Turin, where police used tear gas to break up the crowds. In Rome, police say thousands of people marched from the Colosseum to the ministry of education building where they set fires and were met by police in riot gear.

“This is not a democratic expression of dissent, nor a defense of schools, but an attack on institutions and political hooliganism,” said Minister of Education Giuseppe Valditara, who was the subject of many of the posters.

Other signs showed Meloni and other ministers hanging upside down in a nod to the demise of fascist dictator Benito Mussolini with “killing a fascist is not a crime” written below.

Many protesters held signs that had phrases in French or that said “do it like the French” in solidarity with student protests there.

In several cities, protesters lit trash cans, set off paper bombs — Molotov cocktails — and used fireworks against police. In Turin, many teachers joined the marches.

The day of mobilization came after schools were occupied in Milan, Naples, Turin, Genoa, Bologna and Rome.

Protests have begun this mid-morning local time, in Rennes, Lyon and Marseille, with 40 people detained in the Paris region, according to authorities.

Police used tear gas to disperse crowds in Marseille and Lyon, while the majority of the detentions in Paris were linked to possession of weapons or prohibited protective gear, police said.

Paris police have banned gatherings in a string of locations across Paris, including government sites and train stations.

Speaking this morning on French TV channel Franceinfo, Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Paris suburb Saint-Denis who has become something of a symbolic figurehead for protests, spoke to their objective.

Bagayoko has been applauded for defending students from police on the streets, while some critics have slammed his comments legitimising some violence.

Police violence has come under heavy scrutiny during the weeks-long student lead protests across France, as scores of demonstrators have sustained police-inflicted injuries.

In Paris, riot police appear to have strayed from their typical intimidation tactics with officers advancing towards protesters instead, prompting questions about police tactics and the use of weapons.

Videos of police officers beating students, launching tear gas, water cannon and baton charges at crowds of young people have shocked France in recent weeks.

Images of a teenager in Lens, north France, who reportedly lost a hand to a police grenade and another who was shot in the face with a police tear-gas grenade at near-point-blank range have left many reeling.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez ordered the temporary suspension of one type of stun grenade by police following the loss of the boy’s hand. That ban - which still allowed police to use several different grenades - has now been rescinded.

There have been signs of the police trying a new approach. Some police units have taken to removing their riot helmets to present a softer image, although officers without helmets still clashed with young protesters outside Paris on Friday morning.

While student representatives remain fixed on obtaining tangible results for the education sector, police violence and a government many feel is not listening to them is fuelling the anger of many on the streets.

Given the call for Yellow Vest protestors to join Saturday’s events, there are fears of more violence. Some 900 police officers have been injured in the recent weeks’ protests. According to the interior ministry, only 248 students have been injured, prompting public skepticism.

Some police units have been confiscating handmade signs at protest events, eliciting accusations of limits on free speech. In a conversation with high schoolers organised by French newspaper Le Parisien, Nuñez said that such practices (when signs were not insulting or could not be used as a weapon) was “not normal.”

France is braced for massive protests after weeks of student-led anger on the streets.

But today’s protesters are set to be broader, with the far left, unions, farmers and Yellow Vests having promised to join students Saturday, with some 500 protest events planned nationwide.

Many will be marching in solidarity with the weeks-long student protests, which have faced heavy handed policing.

Calls for protests have also been driven by the high price of gas. Authorities are warning of a “convergence of causes” according to CNN affiliate BFMTV.

Authorities expect up to 100,000 protestors on Saturday outside the capital, with tens of thousands more within Paris. The student-led protests have been the largest in years in France, with no sign yet of an off ramp for the anger coursing through France.

Paris’ police have banned marches targeting Place de la Concorde, which sits beside the presidential palace.

“It’s not normal,” Coppélia Moreau, from the organising committee of the Paris region Interfac student organisation, said Friday of the decision to ban some of the proposed routes, accusing the government of hypocrisy.

Stay with us on this page as we bring you the latest developments.

Resignation" during a gathering near the Gare du Nord train station in Paris in the morning of demonstrations against the cost of living and rising fuel prices called by the "Yellow Vests" movement, joined by French high school and university students, teachers and parents demanding better school conditions and government action, as well as labour unions, workers, farmers and retirees, France, on October 17, 2026.

articles.title: Houthis strike Yemen’s Aden: What that means
articles.summary: What we know about the Houthi strikes on Aden’s presidential palace and airport, and why they matter.
articles.body:
The Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have fired missiles at the presidential palace in the southern Yemeni city of Aden, killing five people and wounding 16, on Thursday.

On Friday, two missiles landed on the grounds of Aden International Airport as a passenger plane prepared to take off for Cairo.

After the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014, the internationally recognised government of Yemen decamped to Aden with the backing of a Saudi-led coalition of Arab countries.

The latest attacks come as Yemen’s war , largely frozen under a 2022 truce, has reignited and become another front in the wider regional conflict involving Iran.

So what has happened in Aden, and why does it matter?

The Houthis hit the Al-Maashiq Presidential Palace with five missiles, according to Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani.

Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said the dead and wounded included guards and civilian employees.

The government said Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and other officials were safe, but two of his bodyguards had been killed.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had struck what he called the “Saudi military operations headquarters” in Aden.

On Friday, two missiles landed on the airport’s grounds, according to the Aden Security Department, which blamed the Houthis. It said it was the second attack on the facility in less than a week.

Yemenia Flight 612 to Cairo was preparing for takeoff. Al-Eryani said the missiles landed about 500 metres (1,600ft) from the aircraft. No casualties were reported.

Al-Eryani called the strike “a direct threat to the lives of passengers and aviation crews”.

The Houthi-run Saba agency claimed the group was targeting a military headquarters and weapons depots inside Badr Camp, a military site next to the airport.

The government moved there after the Houthis took control of the capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government.

The al-Maashiq Palace is the internationally recognised government’s headquarters and its seat of power.

The Houthis currently control much of the country’s north and west. Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi coalition supporting the government had largely ended following a 2022 ceasefire.

But in September, the Houthis launched a lightning offensive along the Red Sea coast, seizing territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Nearly two weeks ago, government forces launched a counteroffensive dubbed “Operation Dawn of Yemen” with Saudi air support, but have so far failed to reverse those gains.

Saree said the Houthi attacks on Aden were part of the group’s declared policy of targeting “Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located”.

In December 2020, an attack on Aden airport as a new cabinet arrived from Saudi Arabia killed at least 22 people.

A second attack hit the palace where ministers had been taken to safety. The coalition blamed the Houthis, who denied responsibility.

On Thursday, Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, blamed Iran for having “encouraged” the escalation.

He said the Iran-backed Houthis had rejected an offer to meet for talks in Oman when the latest round of hostilities began.

Tehran denied the claim on Friday. “The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.

Baghaei said Iran “has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities”, offering again to mediate.

Canada’s embassy in Saudi Arabia condemned the palace attack and called for “an immediate de-escalation of hostilities”.

“We stand in solidarity with the internationally recognised Government of Yemen and the Yemeni people,” the Canadian embassy in Saudi Arabia said in a post on X.

On Thursday, the United Nations Security Council condemned escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including those affecting civil aviation and energy infrastructure.

The governing council of the UN’s International Civil Aviation Organization also condemned recent attacks on civilian airports and aircraft in Saudi Arabia.

On October 9, Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, told the UNSC the country had slid back into “full-scale war”.

What is happening in the wider conflict?

Fighting resumed in July, ending a 2022 truce.

Last month, the Houthis took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most important waterways. Since the Strait of Hormuz was closed by Iran in March amid US strikes, Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on sending oil exports to the Red Sea via its East-West pipeline instead. The Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ships there earlier in the year.

On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, president of the Presidential Leadership Council, announced Operation Dawn of Yemen to retake Houthi-held territory, including Sanaa.

The Saudi-led coalition said 100 fighter jets took part, its first acknowledgement since 2022 that it had resumed air attacks on the Houthis.

The Houthis, in turn, have repeatedly fired missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure.

On Friday, the coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile headed for Yanbu, a Red Sea oil hub which Saudi Arabia has been using to export crude.

On the ground, fighting has intensified in Taiz governorate , where the Houthis have been holding the city of Taiz under siege, and which borders the Red Sea. State-run Saba media outlet, citing the Taiz Axis military command, reported that 168 Houthi fighters had been killed and 210 wounded there.

In Houthi-held areas, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what it called “Saudi aggression” since September 3.

Early on Saturday, Houthi-affiliated media reported attacks east of Saada, with the coalition saying it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers there.

articles.title: Pope Leo to be discharged from hospital today following lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV will leave hospital on Saturday, four days after receiving lung cancer surgery, the Vatican says.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV will leave hospital on Saturday, four days after undergoing lung cancer surgery, the Vatican says, it what will mark a swift return to his duties following the first health scare of his papacy. The 71-year-old first American pope was admitted to the Gemelli hospital on Tuesday with doctors removing a nodule that was determined to be pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. “In light of the blood tests and the chest X-ray performed this morning, and following an assessment of his clinical status, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge,” his doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Prof. Stefano Margaritora, said. The pontiff will likely leave the hospital on Saturday afternoon and return to the Vatican, after celebrating a midday mass at the medical facility. He is due to offer the traditional Sunday blessing from a window overlooking St. Peter’s Square on Sunday, in what will be his first public appearance a week after he told crowds he would be needing surgery. News of the pope’s illness has been met with shock and concern inside the Vatican, while raising questions about what this means for his papacy. Pope Leo was elected last May at the relatively young age of 69 and is in good physical shape. As a cardinal living in Rome, he had a personal trainer and is known to enjoy sports such as tennis and swimming. The pope is scheduled to make a packed trip to Latin America from 6-17 November, including Uruguay, Argentina, and a “homecoming” to Peru where he served as a missionary and bishop for years. The Vatican is remaining cautious about those travel plans. “We need to see how the Pope feels once he is discharged—what his state of health is—and based on that, he will decide whether to keep or cancel his trips,” Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Holy See Secretary of State, told reporters Friday. Since his surgery, however, the pope has worked from the hospital, receiving cardinals and having a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, where he raised the plight of civilians in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky. Past popes have written letters of resignation in case of a severe illness or medical emergency that impedes them from carrying out their duties. Parolin, however, told reporters that he didn’t think Leo had made such a provision. “I don’t think he left anything. It didn’t even seem to me that there was any need and that the matter was so serious to be able to foresee an absence of government.” Just days before his surgery, however, the pope had confirmed Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle as the Dean of the College of Cardinals. The dean, who is the “first among equals” leader of the college, plays a crucial role in presiding over a conclave (providing he’s under 80) and the pre-conclave meetings. Any future papal election is considered far into the future. But the appointment of the 69-year-old Tagle, a charismatic figure previously tipped as a possible pope, was an important piece of housekeeping. This story has been updated.

articles.title: In Portugal, radar and observers shut turbines down during migration; over five autumns, no soaring birds died, though 5,000 crossed the wind farm each year
articles.summary: Discover how radar-assisted shutdown systems in Portugal's Barão de São João wind farm protect soaring birds during migration seasons without halting energy production.
articles.body: The Barão de São João wind farm in the Algarve, in southwestern Portugal, sits on a migratory flyway crossed by soaring birds, including birds of prey, every autumn. Its licence required rigorous mitigation procedures, including a protocol that uses radar and observers to detect approaching birds and shut turbines down when needed. According to a 2017 book chapter by Tomé and colleagues, no soaring birds died from collisions at the wind farm during five consecutive autumn migrations while the protocol was in use.Radar and observers monitored migrating birds.The research team examined the Barão de São João wind farm in the Algarve, in southwestern Portugal. Their findings appeared in the 2017 book chapter Radar Assisted Shutdown on Demand Ensures Zero Soaring Bird Mortality at a Wind Farm Located in a Migratory Flyway, available through Tethys and written by Ricardo Tomé, Filipe Canário, Alexandre Hespanhol Leitão, Nadine Pires and Miguel Repas. The chapter reports that about 5,000 individuals of 30 soaring bird species cross the wind farm every autumn, and that 55% of the soaring birds crossing were recorded at altitudes associated with a high collision risk.To reduce this risk, the wind farm’s licence required a Radar Assisted Shutdown on Demand (RASOD) protocol. Bird migration was observed near the wind farm using radar. Wind turbines were shut down when certain criteria were fulfilled, such as high activity of migration or flying of the threatened bird species. Initially, the shutdown of the wind farm was made at the request of the observation team, but then the team acquired access to the supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) system.Shutdown periods fell from 105 hours to 15 hours.The monitoring program showed that targeted shutdowns could protect soaring birds while keeping interruptions to the wind farm small. According to the chapter, the shutdown period corresponded to 0.2% to 1.2% of the equivalent hours in a year’s wind farm activity. The annual shutdown averaged about 105 hours in the first year and fell to about 15 hours once the monitoring team gained direct access to the turbine control system, which matches the top and bottom of that range. The decrease reflected better coordination and the monitoring team’s growing experience in deciding when shutdowns were necessary.No soaring birds died from collisions during five consecutive autumn migrations. Many of the birds crossed at altitudes that posed a collision risk, which makes that result significant. The procedure targeted soaring birds, so its results do not cover other birds that may pass the turbines. There were also collisions of other types of birds, which were not the primary target of the procedure.Selective shutdowns at 20 Cádiz wind farms cut soaring bird mortality by 61.7%Ferrer and colleagues published a significant decline in Griffon Vulture collision mortality in wind farms during 13-year of a selective turbine stopping protocol in Global Ecology and Conservation in 2022. They analysed 15 years of records for 20 wind farms with 269 turbines in the Cádiz area of southern Spain, from two years before the protocol began in 2008 through 2020. After it began, mortality of soaring birds, mainly raptors and storks, fell by 61.7% and Griffon Vulture mortality fell by 92.8%, with an estimated energy production loss of less than 0.51%. That study covers a different location and operating programme, so its results are not a direct prediction for every wind farm.Targeted shutdowns can support bird conservation.The shorter shutdown times suggest the response became more efficient. Direct access to the turbine controls allowed faster action, and the team’s experience improved its decisions about shutdowns. Radar-guided shutdowns do not eliminate all collision risks, and their effectiveness may depend on bird species, local migration patterns, and the speed of monitoring.You use AI every day. articles.title: Sudan’s army claims dozens of RSF fighters killed in Nyala attack
articles.summary: Rapid Support Forces accuse army of killing 30 civilians in attack on Nyala’s busy livestock market.
articles.body:
The Sudanese army says it has killed dozens of fighters from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in a series of air attacks on the southwestern city of Nyala, but the paramilitary group says the military has killed civilians.

The targets of Friday’s attack were RSF positions and command centres in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state and the seat of the paramilitary group’s self-declared administration, the army said in a statement.

However, the RSF said the army carried out a drone attack on a busy livestock market, killing 30 civilians, including 17 women and five children.

The group has not confirmed or denied whether separate attacks by the army killed some of its fighters and destroyed its command centres.

Separately, the human rights group Emergency Lawyers said in a post on X that a market was hit on Friday in Nyala and the drone used was “affiliated” with the Sudanese army.

Reporting from the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, Al Jazeera’s Almigdad Alruhaid said on Saturday that the fighting between the army and RSF has “intensified”.

“In South Kordofan, a source in the Sudanese government told Al Jazeera that the RSF carried out drone attacks on mining sites with the exchange in fire intensifying in many parts of Sudan in the past 24 hours.”

The army has repeatedly targeted the Darfur region in western Sudan with drones to try to retake territory controlled by the RSF, which holds most of the area.

This month, Sudanese military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan promised to seize “every inch” of territory under RSF control.

The Sudanese civil war began in 2023 and has killed tens of thousands of people. The United Nations has described the situation in Sudan as the world’s worst humanitarian crisis.

articles.title: In 2013, Stephen King and his wife pledged $3 million to save their hometown library; by 2016, the renovation had grown into a $9.6 million project with modern facilities
articles.summary: When novelist Stephen King and his wife, Tabitha King, pledged $3 million to renovate the Bangor Public Library in Maine in 2013, the donation came with a
articles.body: When novelist Stephen King and his wife, Tabitha King, pledged $3 million to renovate the Bangor Public Library in Maine in 2013, the donation came with a condition: the institution had to raise another $6 million. The challenge helped set a wider fundraising effort in motion, with the library meeting its $9 million target in July 2014 before the modernisation project reached $9.6 million by 2016.The story was not simply about a celebrity making a large donation. The Kings’ pledge formed one-third of the proposed fundraising target, requiring the library to secure support from voters, businesses, foundations and individual donors. The result was a project that addressed problems threatening the historic building while introducing facilities intended to make it more useful to the community.A leaking roof prompted the campaignThe Bangor Public Library was confronting a basic but serious problem: its copper roof, installed when the building was constructed in the early 20th century, had developed leaks. Water had entered the building during storms, at one point running down the main staircase. The damage threatened the building and raised concerns about protecting its collection.The library housed more than 500,000 volumes, according to a 2013 Bangor Daily News report. Officials wanted to repair the roof but also improve the building’s interior and make its facilities more practical for readers, staff and community groups.The Kings’ offer was conditional on the library finding the remaining money. Rather than covering the entire project themselves, the couple committed $3 million if the institution could raise another $6 million. The arrangement made the donation a catalyst for a broader campaign, with the library needing to demonstrate that the community and other funders would support the plan.How the library met its $9 million targetThe fundraising effort brought together public funding and private contributions. Bangor voters approved a $3 million bond in June 2013. The Stephen and Tabitha King Foundation pledged $3 million, while the library worked to raise the final $3 million from businesses, foundations and individual donors.In July 2014, the Bangor Daily News reported that the library had met its $9 million fundraising goal. The achievement marked an important turning point: the project could proceed with the money required for the planned work, rather than relying on the Kings’ contribution alone.The Kings’ involvement also reflected an established relationship with the institution. They had donated $2.5 million towards a new library wing in the 1990s. According to the Guardian, they had also paid to replace the library’s front marble steps several years before the 2013 pledge because the worn steps had become dangerous.For King, the library was more than a local building. In a note to his short story 'The Library Policeman', he recalled that a public library had allowed him to read widely as a child from a family with limited means. The experience helps explain why the institution held personal significance for the author, whose novels include 'Carrie', 'The Shining' and 'It'.From structural repairs to modern facilitiesBy August 2016, the renovation had become a $9.6 million modernisation effort. Bangor Daily News reported that the work was nearing completion after several years of construction and disruption to library operations.The changes went beyond repairing the leaking roof. Plans included a glass atrium intended to accommodate a lounge and café, along with a business centre where people could rent workspace by the day, week or month. The children’s wing was moved to the third floor as part of efforts to improve safety.The project sought to preserve the library’s historic role while adapting its spaces for contemporary use. Roof repairs addressed the immediate infrastructure problem, while the redesigned areas offered additional ways for residents to work, read and gather.Construction required temporary disruption, including a partial closure during November and December while some of the most intensive work took place. In August 2016, officials expected the remaining work to finish by the end of September, with a formal dedication planned for the following January.A long-standing connection to MaineThe library pledge was part of a broader pattern of support for the community where the Kings have lived. The Guardian reported in 2013 that King had also contributed to fuel assistance for low-income Maine residents through a local radio fundraiser. He described Bangor as a working-class town and said he and Tabitha were continually looking for ways to help.The library project demonstrates how a conditional philanthropic gift can bring other sources of funding into a community initiative. The Kings’ $3 million commitment did not cover the entire renovation, but it helped establish a fundraising framework that combined a municipal bond, private philanthropy and contributions from other donors.You use AI every day. articles.title: North Dakota ranchers fought a pipeline company over compensation for easements across their land; after spending about $300,000 in legal costs, their fight over who pays those fees is heading to the US Supreme Court
articles.summary: A dispute over who should pay nearly $300,000 in legal expenses has brought a group of North Dakota ranchers and a natural gas pipeline company before the
articles.body: A dispute over who should pay nearly $300,000 in legal expenses has brought a group of North Dakota ranchers and a natural gas pipeline company before the US Supreme Court. The ranchers had challenged the compensation offered for pipeline access across their properties and eventually reached a settlement. However, an appeals court later ruled that the company was not responsible for their legal costs. The Supreme Court is scheduled to hear the case on November 9.The case, Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, concerns Leonard Hoffmann, members of his family and neighbouring ranchers in McKenzie County, according to the official court record. Their disagreement with WBI Energy Transmission began over the amount the company was prepared to pay for easements. These agreements allow a company to use a portion of private land for purposes such as laying and maintaining pipelines without purchasing the entire property.The landowners initially succeeded in getting a court to consider evidence of payments made for similar pipeline easements. A settlement followed, but the legal proceedings had already cost them approximately $300,000. Although the trial court directed WBI to reimburse those expenses, the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit overturned that decision in March 2025.The Supreme Court will now examine whether private companies exercising federally authorised eminent domain powers must follow state compensation laws. According to the Institute for Justice, which represents the ranchers, the case could affect property owners in other states where local laws provide protections beyond the minimum compensation required under the US Constitution.Why the $300,000 legal bill remains disputedThe ranchers' legal expenses became the central issue after their original disagreement with WBI ended in a settlement. They had spent several years challenging how the company calculated the value of the easements.Under North Dakota law, property owners whose land is acquired through eminent domain are entitled to certain protections, including reimbursement of qualifying expenses associated with the proceedings.The trial court applied those provisions and ordered WBI to cover the landowners' legal costs. However, the appeals court changed the decision, saying the company's authority to acquire the easements came from federal law.The Eighth Circuit held that WBI could rely on the compensation rules applicable to the federal government. Those rules do not necessarily require payment of the property owner's legal expenses.The Institute for Justice argues that this interpretation gives private companies protections against state-law requirements that Congress did not expressly grant them.How disagreement over pipeline payments beganThe dispute originated in McKenzie County, a part of western North Dakota where oil and natural gas development has brought extensive pipeline construction.Leonard Hoffmann and neighbouring property owners were already familiar with pipeline easements because oil companies had previously negotiated access to land in the area.However, WBI was developing an interstate natural gas pipeline. Such projects fall under the Natural Gas Act and require approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC).Once a company receives the necessary federal certificate, it can also obtain authority to use eminent domain. This legal power permits the acquisition of private property rights for public use, subject to compensation.WBI proposed that compensation be based on the difference between the value of the land with a pipeline easement and the value of the land without one, the Institute for Justice said. The company argued that the difference could be minimal or even zero.The ranchers believed that this approach did not adequately reflect the value of allowing a pipeline to cross their properties. They wanted the court to consider what other companies had paid landowners for comparable easements.What happened during court proceedingsHoffmann joined his brother David, sister-in-law Denae Hoffmann and neighbouring ranchers Rocky Prestangen and Randy Stevenson in contesting WBI's valuation.They appointed North Dakota property lawyer Derrick Braaten to represent them. The proceedings continued for several years as both sides presented arguments about the appropriate method of determining compensation.The trial court eventually allowed the landowners to introduce evidence from comparable voluntary transactions. This meant payments negotiated between other pipeline companies and property owners could be considered when assessing the value of the easements.Following that decision, the parties reached a settlement. The amount of compensation was no longer the central dispute, but the question of reimbursement for the legal proceedings remained unresolved.WBI challenged the order requiring it to pay those expenses, leading to the March 24, 2025, appellate ruling in its favour.What the Supreme Court will examineThe legal question before the Supreme Court concerns the extent to which federal authority allows a private company to avoid compensation requirements established by individual states.The Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution requires “just compensation” when private property is taken for public use. State laws, however, may provide additional protections, including provisions covering legal expenses.The Institute for Justice maintains that the Natural Gas Act permits qualifying pipeline companies to exercise eminent domain but does not automatically exempt them from state compensation laws.The case has attracted significant attention, with 12 states submitting a brief supporting state-law property protections, while the federal government has presented a different position.You use AI every day.
