articles.title: Exclusive: Inside Erik Prince’s secretive operation taking on Haiti’s gangs
articles.summary: As gangs roam Haiti’s capital, a weakened government has hired Erik Prince to spearhead a military-style crackdown — raising urgent questions about violence, accountability and whether the strategy is working.
articles.body: Trees wrap around buildings, roots sprout from riverbeds of plastic trash, and vines creep down the street. Nature is working to reclaim downtown Port-au-Prince after years of dereliction and gang warfare. But at dawn, through this post-apocalyptic urban forest still come streams of humanity: Hundreds of civilians walk through this dead zone every day, some carrying food, others heading to work — as first light permits them to cross gangland and into what’s left of the city’s free streets. It is a scene of desperation that repeats at dusk, when the same single file of hundreds returns home. Here were once waterfront villas, a cathedral, a busy market frequented by tourists. No one comes here anymore — unless they have no other choice. Years of political turmoil, corruption and the ascendance of a deadly gang coalition are suffocating Haiti’s capital city. The US and international community have repeatedly tried and failed to help bring order. Now, the remnants of Haiti’s government have rolled the dice with a very different option: a US private security tycoon. STREAMING NOW: Haitians are scared to venture out of their homes. Here, life is always on the line. Erik Prince says he can help. Upgrade to watch the full report. Erik Prince and his private security teams were contracted by the US government during the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, most remembered for Blackwater employees opening fire in Baghdad’s Nusoor Square, killing 17 Iraqi civilians. Four of his contractors were convicted in the US and later pardoned by President Donald Trump. Now he’s in Haiti, where his mercenaries are working with elite local police to break the gangs’ chokehold — a secretive project known as the “Task Force.” Prince has also introduced drone warfare to Haiti, with over 2,000 strikes since the Task Force began its operation last March. One seen by CNN shows a tiny drone flying straight into what looks like a water tank on a roof. It ruptures, and then suddenly the building is aflame — a strike on what a Task Force source said was a gang factory for Molotov cocktails. “Insurgencies are not defeated by taking out just leadership,” Prince said last month, in an exclusive interview with CNN in Port-au-Prince. “I know there’s been obsession of that in the United States, but wars are won by taking significant numbers of enemy manpower off the battlefield.” “They are evil criminals and the best place for them is in the ground.” It’s an approach that critics say defies international law and due process. But for many Haitians exhausted by years of gang atrocities, the more important question is: Is it working? A secretive project Prince’s new company Vectus Global was hired by Haiti’s interim government last year. The Task Force now works in a fractured security landscape that includes the Haitian National Police, the new UN-mandated Gang Suppression Force, Haiti’s long-neglected army and a network of armed vigilante groups. Soft-spoken in person but prolific on social media, Prince touts his work in Haiti as a model to other failing states with their own intractable security problems. “When we started, a police truck was lost every week — attacked, ambushed, burned, the occupants slaughtered, butchered,” Prince said, standing on a rooftop overlooking gang-held parts of the capital. “That’s done now, because there’s much better response, quicker air support, drones, whatever, that prevents the police from being overmatched.” Promised milestones have been elusive. When his contract was announced early last year, Prince said he aimed to free up key roads within a year, making it possible to drive from the northern port city of Cap Haitien to Port-au-Prince. Eighteen months on, the vital route remains strangled by gang checkpoints. International flights to Port-au-Prince are stopped because of the risk of being shot over gang territory. General elections were supposed to be held in December; they have been postponed indefinitely. Nonetheless, the past year has, at the least, halted the gangs’ advance in the capital, according to one assessment. The United Nations, which monitors the situation on the ground with quarterly updates, said in September that security operations “have contributed to halting the expansion of gangs in Port-au-Prince and cleared some areas from gang control, including in downtown.” The death toll remains high. Of the 5,700 people killed or injured in 2026, more than half were casualties around security operations, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said in early October. The gangs are also changing their strategies. They’re accelerating into other parts of the country, including farming communities that feed the nation. Forcible recruitment of children has tripled over the past year — between 30% and 50% of gang members are now minors, UNICEF estimates. When gangs come under attack, they leave their youngest members behind with orders to fight until the end, one police commander told CNN. An operation in Kenscoff In the mists of the steep hills that ring southern Port-au-Prince, CNN saw one Task Force operation where helicopters manned by foreign contractors assaulted gang positions, and drones detonated amid the clatter of gunfire. Earlier this summer, a gang had massacred at least 47 residents and kidnapped dozens more in the town of Kenscoff, on the main southern route out of the capital. It was an apparent attempt to gain leverage over the Task Force, with the gang leader releasing a video threatening to kill hostages if drones hurt his troops. The gang eventually released its hostages but dug into the tiny nearby hamlet of Bois D’Avril, into which Prince’s foreign ex-special forces flew in September, engaging them in an hours-long firefight. Footage obtained by CNN showed the Haitian National Police’s SWAT unit entering the village, machine-gunfire in the background, and the distant thud of explosions. It also provided a rare sighting of some of Prince’s men, chatting with a SWAT officer who says, “I have heard a lot of things about you.” A heavily armed foreign contractor points out to the officer a hillside building as a good security position. “We will be around the next few days to help you out,” he says, in an apparent Australian accent. It was an operation that local residents cheered, rushing in to burn gang barricades after police declared the area clear. But for now, it’s still too dangerous for the area’s residents to return home. Many are now refugees in their own country, adding to the more than 1.5 million people who are internally displaced in Haiti — about a tenth of the national population. “I’ve been left with nothing,” said one Kenscoff refugee, Luckson Alfrezin, from a cramped encampment in the capital, after the gang killed his uncles, cousins and aunts, and livestock. “It’s like being a car with no lights on. You’re living but you don’t see why. You are already dead.” A central question is how Haiti’s patchwork forces will hold and defend reclaimed areas like Kenscoff. It’s a role beyond what Prince’s small force is designed to do, but where coordination with the still-growing Gang Suppression Force and Haitian National Police is evolving. How much is Prince getting paid? Prince would not disclose the annual fee he receives for work with the Task Force, claiming only that it is a “fraction” of the cost of the short-lived Multinational Security Support mission — an initiative backed financially and logistically by the United States, that once envisaged 5,500 foreign police in Port-au-Prince. “Our cost is one-sixth of what their annual camp cost was,” Prince said. The sum is likely in the tens of millions of dollars. His income will be augmented by a deal to help control Haiti’s porous border with the Dominican Republic for the next 10 years in return for 10% of any new customs revenue collected. The long-term contract has raised criticism locally of how Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé is using his mandate as interim leader. Human rights lawyer Rosy Auguste Ducena, who advocates for the rights of victims of violence, says the Haitian public is fed up with the slow pace of change. “Absence and inaction are still the biggest issue with all the security forces operating in Haiti,” she said, pointing out that no major gang leader has been killed in years. So far, the Vectus contractors are perceived as “useless,” she added. “First of all, we don’t notice them, that’s the main thing: We don’t see them. And we know they’re very costly because it’s still our taxes that pay them and we don’t see the results,” she added, calling for greater accountability from all the security forces operating in the country. Armed groups still operate with “relative impunity” in Haiti, according to Ducena — a fact underlined by dozens of gang social media accounts flaunting their money, weapons, and freedom of movement, in addition to gruesome torture and kidnapping videos. Deadly drone strikes force gangs to pay attention Prince’s drones have had two palpable effects. First, ordinary people have been caught in some of the blasts. The UN counts 85 civilians dead from drone strikes across Haiti, according to a CNN tally of UN reporting, and directly attributes this to a “private military contractor.” Accounting is patchy, however, and rights workers say some deaths may go unreported because of difficulties they have reaching the kinds of gangland areas targeted by drones. The most prominent case was a failed strike on a gang leader’s birthday party in September last year. At least eight children were among the dozen or more people killed when a drone’s explosive fell in the wrong location. “Everybody started running and screaming. A drone had fallen behind the square where the gang leader was having a party, at the soccer field,” said one woman to CNN, whose 6-year-old daughter was among the dead. “When I rushed to see, I found my child dead, face on the ground.” Prince acknowledges that accidents are “not impossible,” but declined to comment on specific cases. His team runs “dozens of hours of surveillance in an area before we do anything there — a patrol, a raid, or certainly a drone strike,” he added. The second impact of the drone strikes has been to force the gangs to take note. CNN spoke to several gang members in the downtown area of BelAir, where armed men roam the streets openly. They don’t flinch when armored police patrol vehicles pass by, but are wary of the drone threat. One of them, who gave him name as Etienne, told CNN that “drones are pushing us out of the area.” A gang lieutenant, Julio, had a message for Prince. “The biggest threat is Erik Prince’s force,” he said, claiming that if the American left “tomorrow,” it would create a need for peace and dialogue with Haiti’s National Police. “We armed men need peace too. Imagine, I have a wife and kids,” he said from behind his camouflage balaclava, his subordinates holding batons and guns around him. Dialogue and disarmament have been floated before in Haiti, but sources say attempts to gauge interest from the main gang coalition Viv Ansanm (“Live Together” in Haitian Creole) have so far fallen flat.And while Haiti has committed to a handover protocol for child gang members, getting the public to accept reintegration of anyone with gang associations is likely to be challenging. That may be why Prince seems so confident in the brutal fix he’s offering. “I welcome all those critics to come and walk through the rough neighborhoods of Port-au- Prince for a week or a day and see how long they last,” he said.

articles.title: ChinaAid raises alarm over imprisoned Chinese pastor's health as family seeks answers
articles.summary: ChinaAid founder Bob Fu says reports of Pastor Wang Yi's advanced liver cancer in a Chinese prison are credible but cannot be independently verified.
articles.body: The founder of Christian human rights organization ChinaAid is raising concerns over the health of an imprisoned Chinese pastor who may be suffering from advanced liver cancer, as his family continues to face restrictions on visitation adn access to medical information. Rev. Dr. Bob Fu, founder and president of ChinaAid, told Fox News in an interview that reports concerning Pastor Wang Yi's health are "very worrying," citing information received from multiple sources inside China. Wang, the founding pastor of Early Rain Covenant Church in Chengdu, has been imprisoned since December 2018 and is serving a nine-year sentence on charges of inciting subversion of state power and illegal business operations. Although Fu believes that reports of advanced liver cancer are credible, he acknowledged that his organization has not been able to independently confirm the diagnosis. REPORT DETAILS RISING PRESSURE ON UNDERGROUND CATHOLICS AS CHINA DENIES CRACKDOWN Fu said ChinaAid was "not able to really independently verify" the reports, citing restrictions on access to Wang and the absence of an independent medical examination. The organization first publicly raised concerns about Wang's condition on Sept. 28, calling on Chinese authorities to provide his family with access to him and disclose information about his medical treatment. During the interview, Fu revealed that authorities reportedly provided information by telephone about medical examination they claimed had been conducted on Oct. 1. According to Fu, prison officials cited medical information indicating Wang was in good health. However, his family has not been permitted a new in-person visit to independently assess his condition. Fu said that despite repeated letters from Wang's wife and relatives requesting access, "no meeting had been granted at all," since the latest health concerns emerged. The pastor's church has also expressed uncertainty about his condition. TRUMP SHOULD PRESS XI ON CHINA’S PERSECUTION OF BELIEVERS AT HOME AND ABROAD In an Oct. 3 open letter, Early Rain Covenant Church acknowledged the reports but said it could not determine whether Wang had fallen ill. The church called on prison authorities to permit regular family visits, correspondence and telephone calls, as well as provide information about any necessary medical care. According to the church, Wang's family has been permitted fewer than five visits during nearly eight years of imprisonment. Fu likewise described severely restricted visitation, saying meetings have been brief and closely monitored by authorities. He alleged that discussions concerning Wang's health or religious beliefs have resulted in visits being abruptly terminated. "Two years, not a single letter for his wife," Fu said, describing the restrictions on communication. "That's not acceptable. That's even a violation of its own law." Wang was arrested on Dec. 9, 2018, during a crackdown on Early Rain Covenant Church, an independent Protestant congregation operating outside China's state-regulated religious systems. In December 2019, a Chinese court sentenced him to nine years in prison. The U.S. State Department condemned the conviction at the time, describing the prosecution as connected to Wang's peaceful advocacy for religious freedom and calling for his release. The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom currently lists Wang as a religious prisoner of conscience and has documented reports of medical neglect. Fu also raised concerns about the treatment of Wang's wife Jiang Rong, who was detained during the initial crackdown. He said Jiang had previously been subjected to residential surveillance at a police-arranged location, rather than being allowed to remain in her own home, and described the lasting emotional consequences of her treatment. Fu said he believes the severity of the reports warrants immediate action, particularly given the limited access to Wang. He called on the Chinese authorities to permit Wang's wife, son and elderly parents to meet with him privately, allow an independent medical examination in the presence of legal counsel, and release his medical records, including information concerning medications administered during his imprisonment. Fu also expressed concern about reports of mistreatment of other prisoners of conscience, including allegations of forced medication and serious physical and psychological harm. Those allegations were discussed as part of his broader concerns about the treatment of detainees in China, rather than as established evidence of what has happened to Wang. PENCE COMMENDS TRUMP FOR WINNING FREEDOM OF BEIJING'S ZION CHURCH PASTOR EZRA JIN FROM CHINESE DETENTION The ChinaAid president urged the Trump administration to raise Wang's case directly with Chinese officials during upcoming diplomatic engagements. "I really want to see the Trump administration to continue to speak up forcefully," Fu told Fox News, calling for the names of individual prisoners of conscience to be included in high-level discussions. He pointed to the July release of Pastor Ezra Jin Mingri, who was reunited with his family after President Donald Trump raised his case with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a May visit to Beijing. Fu believes that example demonstrates the potential importance of direct diplomatic intervention, although the circumstances of Jin's release do not establish that such pressure would produce the same result in Wang's case. Trump and Xi are expected to attend upcoming international summits, including the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leader's meeting in Shenzhen, China, in November and the G-20 summit in Miami in December. Fu urged U.S. leaders not to allow trade and security negotiations to overshadow concerns about religious freedom, human rights and the treatment of prisoners. "I think it's time to hold them accountable," Fu said. In a statement to Fox News, Chinese Embassy spokesperson Liu Chang said the embassy had no information to provide regarding Wang's specific case. The spokesperson defended China's religious policies, saying the government protects freedom of religious belief under Chinese law and does not interfere in religious groups' internal affairs. Liu added that China prohibits illegal activities carried out under the guise of religion and opposes foreign interference in its domestic affairs. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The embassy did not directly address questions about Wang's reported medical condition, family visitation or the possibility of an independent medical examination. The U.S. State Department did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment by publication time.

articles.title: In South Africa, researchers painted two red stripes on one turbine blade; a preprint suggests bird fatalities fell by a median 83% at four treated turbines
articles.summary: A recent study in South Africa shows that painting red stripes on wind turbine blades can significantly reduce bird fatalities, with a reported median decrease of 83%. This innovative approach offers a promising solution to protect avian species while harnessing wind energy.
articles.body: Wind turbines offer a cleaner alternative to fossil fuels, but their rotating blades can pose a collision risk to birds, including raptors that hunt or soar near wind farms. Researchers in South Africa have tested a simple way to address this problem by painting two broad red stripes on one blade of selected turbines. According to a 2026 preprint on red-patterned wind turbine blades, the experiment at the Umoya wind farm near Hopefield in South Africa's Western Cape found a median 83% reduction in bird fatalities at four treated turbines. The approach aims to make moving blades more visible to birds, potentially helping them avoid collisions without requiring turbines to be stopped. However, the findings remain preliminary, and further trials are needed to establish whether the method works consistently across different wind farms and bird species.How researchers tested the red stripesThe study, titled Crouching tiger, hidden dangers: Avian fatality rates reduced by red-blade patterning at a species-rich African wind farm, examined a 37-turbine facility in a region known for its rich birdlife. For 2023, two large Signal Red stripes were painted on one rotor blade at each of four wind turbines known to kill the highest number of birds. The rest of the turbines remained as they were originally. These stripes were supposed to provide more contrast between the moving blades and their background environment. Each stripe was about a quarter of the blade’s length, with a white section between them. The red colour was chosen in part because South African civil aviation regulations restrict the use of black paint.Bird mortality data were collected before and after treatment through an experiment involving four neighbouring turbines, along with another set of 12 control turbines. This allowed them to test whether mortality was lower at the patterned turbines than at the control turbines. The observation period lasted 32 months, beginning when the patterned turbines were installed in April 2023. Statistical models were used to measure the impact of treatment, taking into account the differences between the two turbine types.What the results revealedThe results showed a substantial difference between the treated and untreated turbines. Over 32 months, 25 bird fatalities were recorded across the 20 turbines included in the comparison, with two occurring at the four turbines with patterned blades and 23 at the 16 untreated control turbines. Bayesian analysis estimated a median 83% reduction in bird fatality rates at the patterned turbines. However, the estimate had wide credible intervals, ranging from 14% to 98% when compared with the four nearest-neighbour controls and from 30% to 97% when compared with all 16 control turbines.Another question is whether birds that avoid the painted blades might collide with nearby unpainted turbines. The South African study found little evidence of an increase in fatalities at neighbouring turbines, although the small sample size meant that this possibility could not be ruled out conclusively. These findings are consistent with a 2020 study published in Ecology and Evolution. Conducted at Norway's Smøla wind farm, the research found that painting one of a turbine's three blades black reduced the annual bird fatality rate by 71.9% compared with neighbouring unpainted turbines.The researchers also found no evidence that birds avoiding the painted turbines were being redirected towards nearby unpainted ones. The South African experiment extended this approach to a more species-rich setting, using red stripes rather than a solid black blade. The contrast may have made the moving blades easier for birds to detect, while the colour itself may also have played a role. However, the experiment did not establish which visual feature was primarily responsible for the reduction in fatalities.A promising step, but more evidence is neededThe appeal of blade patterning is that it is relatively simple. While a radar detection system or automatic shut-down mechanism relies on constant monitoring, the painted blades do not. The scientists proposed that this method could provide an effective way of lowering the number of birds killed in wind farms without resorting to more costly methods. However, painting turbine blades is itself a difficult task. Special equipment may be required to paint the blades of the turbines installed at heights above the ground, and it should be done in proper conditions. The painting process could perhaps be incorporated into turbine blade production.There were only four turbines used in the treatment, and the report was issued as a preprint article in May 2026; consequently, the research had not been formally peer-reviewed when it was published. Further experimentation with larger samples and in different terrains, climates, and bird populations is needed before the decrease can be treated as a general finding. For now, the experiment offers an encouraging sign that wind farms may be able to reduce bird deaths.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Solar power booms in Philippines as war on Iran spikes energy costs
articles.summary: With Southeast Asia’s largest electricity bills rising even higher, Filipinos invest in rooftop panels.
articles.body:
Manila, Philippines – Keith Cantera and his family have been thinking about having their own solar power grid at home for years. But spending up to $5,000 for solar panels was nothing to scoff at, so they put the idea on the back burner.

It all changed this year when the United States-Israel war on Iran rattled global energy markets and sent electricity prices soaring. From paying a monthly bill of about $150 before the war began in late February, Cantera said his family went to forking out as much as $220.

Eight months later, they are having solar panels installed on their rooftop.

“The cost is about the same as paying our electric bills for three or four years based on the current rate,” Cantera said. “But in the fifth year, we’ll have recovered our investment, and electricity will essentially be free.”

Cantera is one of a growing number of Filipino homeowners turning to solar power in a country that had Southeast Asia’s highest electricity costs even before the war. They were comparable only to Singapore, where the average income is more than 10 times higher.

A report by the energy think tank Ember estimated that rooftop panels had nearly doubled in the Philippines since early 2025.

And in the first months of the war from March to May, the rush for solar power led to $407m in panel imports, according to government trade data from China, where most panels are manufactured. The Philippines became the biggest single overseas market for that period. Only the Netherlands bought more, but it redistributes them to the rest of Europe.

Lexus Grepo, CEO of the solar power supplier Solarmaxx, can attest to the boom.

“There is a 30-day wait because solar panel shipments can’t keep up,” Grepo said. “In March, we had 40 projects, which was almost triple our monthly clientele. Since then, we have been setting up 25 to 30 systems a month.”

Grepo does not expect demand to slow down even if tensions in the Middle East ease and shipping routes for energy supplies reopen.

“I think people now realise that the world is an unpredictable place, so they have to be ready for any eventuality. Filipinos now see that they don’t necessarily have to be at the mercy of the global energy market.”

The Philippines, one of the few countries in the region where electricity is not subsidised, relies on imported coal and gas for more than 70 percent of its power mix. The value of its currency, the peso, which has slid to a record low of more than 63 to the US dollar, is making these imports even costlier.

In late March, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr declared a national energy emergency in response to the war ⁠and what he described as the “imminent danger” posed to the national energy supply. Still, electricity rates have continued to increase.

The shift to solar is also partly driven by anger at electric companies that have come under scrutiny for charging customers for so-called system losses, which include illegal connections.

Cantera said learning about having to pay for someone else’s electricity consumption was the last straw.

“Who would agree to paying for something that you did not use? It’s not like the money we spend for electricity just fell from heaven,” he added.

But while the soaring demand is real, the upfront cost of a solar power system is still too high for most Filipinos. The government in March launched a new initiative offering loans for residential rooftop installations, but these are available only to public sector workers.

What officials hope can bring power rates down for the majority of people are the dozens of renewable energy projects in the pipeline, including a 3,500-hectare (8,650-acre) solar farm north of the capital, Manila, that is projected to be the largest in the world. When fully operational, the project is expected to generate 850 megawatts of electricity for 2.4 million households.

But some consumers said such projects could take years to complete, leaving them with ballooning electricity bills unless they take action themselves.

“It’s just so unpredictable nowadays. You have the impending El Nino weather pattern. There’s still war, the continuing fuel price hikes and so much more,” Cantera said. “So why not utilise a natural resource?”

articles.title: Pope Leo to be discharged from the hospital after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV will be discharged from the hospital on Saturday after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous nodule from his right lung, the Vatican said, and will make an appearance to lead prayer on Sunday.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV will be discharged from the hospital on Saturday after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous nodule from his right lung, the Vatican said, and will make an appearance to lead prayer on Sunday. “Following the conclusions reached by the medical team this morning, Pope Leo XIV will be discharged today from Gemelli Polyclinic Hospital, where he was admitted for surgery on his right lung,” the Holy See Press said Saturday in a statement. “He will leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican,” it added. He was expected to recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment at St. Peter’s Basilica on Sunday, according to the statement. The pontiff’s personal doctor, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said that in light of blood tests and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning, and after an assessment of his clinical condition, “the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge from the hospital.” So far, Leo’s doctors have given no indication that the pontiff might need any further treatment. And the Vatican has not indicated whether the cancer might have spread. Leo, who is a Chicago native, resumed working from the hospital on Thursday, his doctors and the Vatican reported. The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Leo since his surgery, showing him celebrating Mass inside the hospital, as doctors said that tests confirmed the “continued improvement” in his recovery. The photos show Leo standing up at the altar in green vestments celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel that has been set up for him. Spokesman Matteo Bruni said he presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily. His discharge from the hospital comes less than a month before Leo is scheduled to jet off for a two-week trip to South America, which is set to start Nov. 11. Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, in an interview on Peruvian television, said the pace of the pope’s recovery could determine whether Leo makes his weeklong apostolic visit to Peru. “I want the pope to know that here in Peru, millions of us are praying for his speedy recovery,” Fujimori said Wednesday. Leo was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer, after doctors examined the nodule they had removed from his right lung. Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 80% of all cases of the disease, according to the American Lung Association. This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker. The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer last week. Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli Hospital as he entered Tuesday. The procedure was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, with medical staff reciting the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel as the operation began.

articles.title: Edvard Munch print found at Kent estate to be auctioned in London
articles.summary: A print by artist Edvard Munch has emerged from a Kent family collection after more than 50 years.
articles.body:
A print by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch that has remained in the same family for more than 50 years is expected to sell for up to £80,000 at auction.

The work, Melancholy III, was discovered at a private estate in north Kent and was listed to be sold by Catherine Southon Auctioneers in London on 28 October.

Created in 1902, the artwork was found with its original receipt showing it was bought in Norway in 1969 for 42,000 Norwegian kroner, the equivalent to about £3,300 in recent exchange rates.

The woodcut, which was printed from a carved block, shows a person near the sea, contrasting with the apparent intimacy of a couple walking towards a rowing boat, according to the auction house.

Catherine Southon, the owner of the auction house in Chislehurst, said: "It is always exciting to discover a work of this calibre emerging from a private family collection, particularly when it has remained with the same family for more than half a century.

"What makes this discovery especially compelling is the survival of the original 1969 purchase receipt, which gives us a wonderful glimpse into the work's history and the moment it first entered the family's care."

Auctioneers described the piece as "an early impression of one of Munch's best-known themes".

Munch was known for showing emotions such as anxiety, loneliness, jealousy and despair, captured in his best-known work The Scream.

Southon said while The Scream remained his most famous expression of anguish, Melancholy III revealed a "quieter" vision, exploring themes of loneliness and unrequited love.

The scene in the artwork was set on the shoreline at Asgardstrand, a coastal town where Munch spent many of his summers.

Southon said the work, which was signed by the artist, was especially interesting because of the way it was made.

Munch used two oak blocks, with one carrying the carved design and a separate "colour block" cut into sections for the sky, sea and shore, she said.

The print has been given a sale estimate of £50,000 to £80,000.

articles.title: In 2024, Brad Paisley and Kimberly Williams-Paisley put $1 million toward a second free grocery store; two years later, the Nashville site opened so families could choose food without paying
articles.summary: In August 2024, country music star Brad Paisley and his wife, actor Kimberly Williams-Paisley, pledged the first $1 million towards a $5 million campaign
articles.body: In August 2024, country music star Brad Paisley and his wife, actor Kimberly Williams-Paisley, pledged the first $1 million towards a $5 million campaign to open a second location of their nonprofit grocery store in Nashville, Tennessee. The new site opened on January 14, 2026, at TriStar Centennial Medical Center, allowing eligible families to select groceries without paying. Reports by Southern Living, TriStar Health and local broadcaster WSMV document the expansion, which aims to help more people facing food insecurity while preserving their dignity and freedom of choice.The store, called The Store, was co-founded by the couple and first opened in March 2020 on the campus of Belmont University, Paisley’s alma mater. Unlike a conventional food pantry, where people may receive pre-packed food boxes, it operates like a grocery store. Referred families can choose from fresh produce, meat, dairy products and pantry staples according to their needs and dietary preferences.The model is designed to make receiving food assistance feel less like accepting a handout and more like an ordinary shopping experience. The organisation works through referrals from nonprofit and government agencies, and its assistance is intended to help people through periods of financial difficulty as they work towards greater stability.From one store to a second locationThe idea behind The Store emerged after the Paisleys volunteered with their two sons at Unity Shoppe, a free supermarket in Santa Barbara, California. The experience helped the family understand how community support could provide essential goods while treating people with dignity, according to the organisation’s account of its origins.The couple subsequently partnered with Belmont University to establish a similar initiative in Nashville. The original store opened on March 12, 2020, just days after a devastating tornado outbreak struck the area and shortly before the Covid-19 pandemic disrupted normal operations. The organisation adapted during the early months of the pandemic, offering curbside collection and home delivery, particularly for older people. It continued developing its services as the needs of local families became clearer.By August 2024, the Paisleys announced plans for a second location in partnership with TriStar Centennial Medical Center. The new site was planned for the ground level of the hospital’s B Garage at 311 23rd Avenue North in Nashville. The expansion campaign aimed to raise $5 million to fund construction and operations, with the couple committing the first $1 million.The partnership also connected food assistance with healthcare. TriStar Centennial’s leadership said some hospital staff had been spending their own money to help patients obtain food and clothing. The new arrangement was intended to create a more organised way to connect people experiencing food insecurity with assistance close to the hospital.Why the expansion matteredThe second store was designed to increase the nonprofit’s capacity at a time when demand was rising. WSMV reported in January 2026 that the original location had served 2,200 families in 2025 and had developed a substantially longer waiting list. The broadcaster also reported a 40% increase in families facing food insecurity over the preceding year, citing the local situation as a key reason for the expansion.The new store is nearly three times the size of the original location, according to reporting around its opening. Its larger footprint provides additional room for grocery shopping, storage and volunteers, while the location is expected to allow the organisation to serve more than twice as many families as before.The second site also offers emergency clothing, extending assistance beyond food. The organisation’s broader services include support such as counselling, nutrition education, cooking classes and financial planning. These programmes are intended to help shoppers manage immediate needs while working towards longer-term stability.The new location officially opened on January 14, 2026, with Paisley and Williams-Paisley joining hospital and city leaders for a ribbon-cutting ceremony. The opening allowed the nonprofit to begin reaching people who had been waiting for assistance through the original Belmont University site.Dignity and choice at the centreFor the Paisleys, the purpose of the project extends beyond providing groceries. The Store’s model lets shoppers make their own selections rather than receive identical food packages, allowing households to choose items that fit their circumstances. That distinction can matter for families with different dietary requirements, children, older relatives or limited cooking facilities. Access to fresh food, meat and dairy also broadens the choices available to shoppers.The organisation relies on donations, staff and volunteers to keep the stores operating. It reported that more than 3,100 volunteers supported its work in 2025, helping stock shelves, assist shoppers and run year-round programmes. With the second location open, it said it would need around 275 volunteers each week.The expansion does not mean the need for assistance has disappeared. Local reporting indicated that the waiting list had grown as demand increased, even before the new store began operating. The larger site is intended to increase capacity, but the organisation continues to depend on donations and volunteers to maintain its services.The $1 million pledge in 2024 was therefore the beginning of a wider community effort, rather than the sole funding source for the project. By combining the couple’s contribution with other donations and a partnership with TriStar Centennial, The Store opened a second site in 2026, extending a grocery model built around free food, personal choice and the dignity of families seeking help.You use AI every day. articles.title: Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist
articles.summary: The French royal jewel will be on public display for the first time since it was found hidden in an apple after a 1926 theft.
articles.body:
A rare pink diamond is going on display in France for the first time since it was stolen almost 100 years ago to the day - the last time it was shown to the public.

The nine-carat, pear-shaped gemstone known as the "Grand Condé" was pilfered in an overnight raid on the Château de Chantilly in October 1926 and concealed in a hollowed-out apple.

The diamond - one of few royal jewels to survive the French Revolution - was recovered a few weeks later when a hungry maid at the hotel in which the thieves were staying took a bite of the apple.

It will once again be on display in the Condé Museum at the Château de Chantilly until 3 January.

The museum's director Mathieu Deldicque said that while the apple story may sounds far-fetched, it was widely covered by newspapers at the time.

Deldicque has faced questions about whether the exhibition may be tempting fate, especially given the string of heists on European cultural institutions in the past 12 months, including the daring daylight robbery of jewellery from the Louvre museum in Paris.

While he declined to reveal to CNN how much the diamond was insured for, he noted that extensive academic study into the properties of the diamond had taken place to make it uniquely identifiable.

The results of this analysis, as well as previously unseen archive material about the gem's history and theft, form part of the exhibition, according to the museum.

Naturally occurring pink diamonds are exceptionally rare and often sell for tens of millions of dollars. The highest price ever fetched for one at auction was $71.2m (£53.6m) in 2017, according to Sotheby's.

The exact origins of the Grand Condé remain a mystery.

It was first mentioned in 1740 in an inventory of Louis Henri de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, drawn up following his death, the Château de Chantilly said.

It then became part of the collection of Queen Marie-Amélie of Bourbon-Sicily, the wife of French King Louis Philippe I, and then her son, Prince Henri of Orléans, the Duke of Aumale.

He bequeathed it to the Institut de France, which now owns the Château de Chantilly, 50km (31 miles) north of Paris, along with thousands of artworks and manuscripts which became the Musée Condé collection.

articles.title: Hasan Piker's influence tests breaking point of Democratic Party
articles.summary: Hasan Piker's Twitch influence is reshaping Democratic Party politics as DSA-aligned candidates gain momentum ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
articles.body: Ahead of the midterm elections, one name has repeatedly surfaced in conversations about the future of the Democratic Party: Hasan Piker. The political commentator streams for hours each day on Twitch, promoting socialism, criticizing Israel and the U.S. and discussing the news of the day from his far-left perspective. But as Piker has gone from a niche online commentator to a real-life player in Democratic politics, his growing involvement has raised questions about what his influence could mean for the future of the party. While Piker's Twitch streams are viewed by tens of thousands daily, his online reach is not what has drawn the questions about the future of the party; rather, it is how engaged his followers are. "It's very clear to me that the people who do love and support him, really love and support him. So, the followers that he has are super loyal and I think they're really active, and they're very engaged," Isaac Saul, founder of the non-partisan politics newsletter Tangle, told Fox News Digital. OCASIO-CORTEZ CALLS FOCUS ON HASAN PIKER 'ABSOLUTELY LUDICROUS' AS SOME DEMOCRATS DEMAND DISTANCE Piker's followers are mostly young people, a demographic Saul called a "prized possession for the Democratic Party." He explained that Democrats were eager to hold onto young voters "because if they can turn out younger voters, that's going to increase their odds of winning in all manner of elections that happen in American politics." Mark Penn, a longtime Democratic pollster who served as an adviser to former President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, similarly pointed to Piker's appeal to young voters, describing him as almost a "Pied Piper." However, Penn questioned how closely those voters actually align with the streamer's views. "Nobody could possibly agree with the garbage that Hasan Piker says. It's anti-American, it's antisemitic, it's anti virtually anything, it's anti-having any decorum, sensibility, or intellectual component beyond kind of throwing everything and everyone overboard. So, the whole thing is nihilistic," Penn told Fox News Digital. STEPHEN A SMITH WARNS HASAN PIKER WILL ‘CONTAMINATE’ DEMOCRATS IN THE MIDTERMS, ‘COME BACK TO HAUNT THEM’ Saul recently outlined his positions on Piker in a piece titled, "My honest thoughts on Hasan Piker." He told Fox News Digital that readers asked him repeatedly, "What's your beef with Hasan Piker?," prompting him to explain his position fully. Saul started his piece by stating that he believes "Piker is a bad guy" and said that he doesn't "trust" the Twitch streamer. Saul sees Piker as a "big pariah" within the Democratic establishment, even as he gains prominence. The Tangle founder believes, however, that the 2026 midterm elections could shift the party's perspective on Piker and the influence of the far left. HASAN PIKER VOWS HE WILL PRESSURE JAMES TALARICO TO GOVERN AS A LEFTIST, NOT A MODERATE "I still view him as kind of an outsider-y person trying to throw his weight around. I think the 2026 midterm has the potential to change that because Piker has endorsed some of the more progressive kind of DSA-type candidates, and if we see them win in House or Senate races, he said, 'We're gonna hold them accountable,'" Saul told Fox News Digital. Penn also sees the midterms as a potential test of Piker's influence, specifically in the Michigan U.S. Senate race where he was involved with Abdul El-Sayed's campaign. Beyond Piker, Penn sees the midterms as an evaluation of the effectiveness of socialist movements. "Obviously, I think the Michigan race is a big test case on all of this. I think that if El-Sayed wins in Michigan, then that will be a huge boost to these movements, to people like Piker and all of the outlandishness that they stand for because it wins elections," Penn told Fox News Digital. "If there's a setback here and a setback on the headline elections in Maine, Michigan, and Texas, then maybe the Democrat party is going to come much more to its senses and say these 'movements really didn't work.'" KYRSTEN SINEMA QUESTIONS WHETHER MODERATES STILL HAVE A PLACE IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY While Saul and Penn see the midterms as a test of whether Piker can leverage his online popularity into real-world results, others argue that the shift is already happening, pointing to the growing number of candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Julian Epstein, a former chief counsel for Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee, told Fox News Digital that he believes mainstream Democrats are underestimating the influence of Piker and the left-leaning movement behind him. "I think that the lie a lot of moderate Democrats are telling themselves is that you're only going to see 10, 12 members of Congress that fall under the DSA banner, and I think that's delusion," Epstein told Fox News Digital. "I think what you're increasingly seeing is that the socialist movement and the far-left movement is becoming the beating heart of the Democratic Party. Why? Because that's where all the activist energy is, and we saw that with the primaries." Mainstream and moderate Democrats, according to Epstein, are "scared of this movement" and that they are not willing to fight against it. "Democrats are increasingly scared to take this movement on because they fear the flying monkeys of the online left," he said. Epstein also argues that establishment Democrats have lost control of the party. He said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and other establishment Democrats have ceased being leaders and are increasingly turning into "marionettes of the far-left." While Epstein believes Piker appeals to "very frustrated" voters who "want to burn down the system," Saul sees some of the streamer's more mainstream views as part of the key to his popularity. INSIDE HASAN PIKER’S RADICAL VIEWS ON AMERICA, ISRAEL AND SOCIALISM "Hasan Piker supports Medicare for all. He wants to abolish cash bail. He thinks big agriculture needs to be broken up. He wants to renegotiate our relationship with Saudi Arabia. I mean, I think those ideas are not just broadly popular with progressives, but popular probably with some people in the populist MAGA right," Saul told Fox News Digital. "I think he could become an influential figure. If there was more momentum in Congress to make some of those policy prescriptions law." As some Democrats attempt to reach Piker's young audience, they could risk losing voters who already feel that the party has gone too far to the left. JAMES CARVILLE VOWS TO ABANDON DEMOCRATIC PARTY IF FAR-LEFT HASAN PIKER BECOMES LEADING VOICE Penn noted that political parties could have much more to gain by saying no to extreme movements than going along with them. "So much time is spent on turnout and base and not enough realization that if I said no to the extremes, I could get a lot of those voters in the middle to switch. And those are twice as powerful as getting those extreme movements," Penn said. Tanya Tsikanovsky, a former Democrat who worked to elect Hillary Clinton in 2016 before later leaving the party, told Fox News Digital that she believes the Democratic Party's shift to the left is leaving voters like her politically "homeless." "I think that we need to stop focusing on how bad or how maybe salvageable the Democratic Party is and not think about them at all, and instead focus on the independents or on the moderate Democrats, like I once was, that feel completely homeless," Tsikanovsky told Fox News Digital. "Because there are a ton of [Sen. John] Fettermans and Bill Mahers that are gonna really not have anywhere to go soon. Their party is going to be completely eaten up by the DSA." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Tsikanovsky agreed with Epstein's assessment that moderates in the Democratic Party have been left without power amid the rise of DSA candidates across the country. "The DSA candidates and people like Hasan Piker are the ones that are being platformed by that party and the moderate ones don't really have power anymore at all," Tsikanovsky said. The debate over Piker's role in the Democratic Party is at the heart of a larger question about how far left the party is willing to shift in order to gain voters, and how much that change could cost or benefit them. Saul argued that Piker's influence is best understood by viewing his ability to shape the national conversation, rather than seeing him as a politician or activist. Not a journalist, not even an activist. Not a politician, but somebody who is just trying to change the conversation culturally that people are having. And I think, when you do that, he makes a lot more sense," Saul said. Fox News Digital reached out to Hasan Piker and the DSA for comment.

articles.title: ‘Times have changed’: The Italian princess renting out her palace in Rome
articles.summary: In our roundup of travel stories this week: Istanbul’s time-traveling hotel, a slow-eater’s guide to Hong Kong, plus the aristocrats opening their homes to guests.
articles.body: In our roundup of travel stories this week: Istanbul’s time-traveling hotel, a slow-eater’s guide to Hong Kong, plus the aristocrats opening their homes to guests. Palazzo for hire Gone are the days when the duties of an Italian princess involved nothing more than a bit of regal hand-waving and playing piano for guests. Legal recognition of the country’s nobility stopped in 1946 and for aristocrats such as Princess Giacinta Ruspoli, upkeep of the family’s ancestral homes doesn’t come cheap. So Giacinta and her mother, Princess Maria Pia, a former Miss Sicily, rent out Ruspoli Bonaparte Residence, a 16th-century palace in Rome, and greet the paying guests. A night in one of the property’s four suites — each measuring more than 1,000 square feet including several halls, ceiling-high stone fireplaces and marble decorations — starts at about $470, including butler service and breakfast. Guests also get an “entrance ticket” to another noble residence, the family’s Castello Ruspoli, a former hunting estate in a village 30 miles north of Rome, which has been recently renovated to create a 10-suite boutique hotel. “We consider ourselves as mere keepers” of the properties, says Giacinta. “Times have changed. My family wants to share all this beauty we have been gifted with everyone else.” Doing the time warp We all know about leap years, when February 29 is added to help keep our calendars synchronized with the Earth’s orbit around the sun. Since the 1970s, leap seconds have also been doing the job of correcting the imbalance between astronomical time and the ultraprecise atomic clocks that now set the global standard. This week, however, international timekeepers voted to scrap them and introduce the leap hour, the first of which might not happen for thousands of years. Our notion of standardized time is a modern construct, spurred by the advent of rail travel in the 19th century and the need for agreed-upon timetables. The Orient Express was a pioneering international rail service that began in 1883, but its end destination, Turkey, didn’t adopt the Gregorian calendar until more than 40 years later. The country’s first New Year’s party was held at the legendary Pera Palace Hotel. Turkey abolished the Rumi calendar, which was pinned to the year 1341, and instantly woke up in the Western Gregorian year of 1926. It was a literal 585-year chronological leap, executed overnight. Party before breakfast Why wait until nighttime for the fun to start? In London, hundreds of people turned up in the financial district for a Wednesday morning dance-off before work, as appetite grows worldwide for daytime raves. It’s a wholesome wellness trend, where revelers are fueled by nothing more than morning air and good vibes. In London, the morning ravers get the party started quickly before the work day, but in Hong Kong, it’s diners who are focused on speed. In this city, eating fast isn’t just practical – it’s a virtue, an art form and a way of life. However, CNN’s Maggie Wong was raised in Hong Kong by a father who taught her never to rush a meal: Here’s a slow-eater’s guide to navigating the city’s restaurants. North Korean flight attendants CNN’s Will Ripley has made 19 trips to North Korea and used its national airline, Air Koryo, many times. He spoke to a flight attendant to learn more about the job, which gives her a rare opportunity for a North Korean: the ability to travel. In case you missed it In “Christiane Amanpour: Sex & Love Around the World,” the CNN journalist explores global attitudes to intimacy and relationships. CNN subscribers can watch here. They were “crawling over our belongings.” A plane was grounded after a reported bedbugs outbreak. A roller coaster tragedy. A White House appointment. A CNN Town Hall. What do you remember from the week that was? “London pizza” is now a thing. And some say it’s the best in the world.

articles.title: Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas?
articles.summary: Analysts say Russia will benefit most from US sanctions waiver.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has signed an executive order waiving newly-passed Russia sanctions, claiming the move is in the US’s “national interest”.

Earlier this month, Trump also announced a deal to bring stocks of Russian diesel into global markets, in a bid to drive down energy prices that have spiked during the US-Israel war on Iran. The US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027.

Trump’s embrace of Russian energy has angered Ukraine, European partners and many US officials, who say the move rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war against its neighbour.

Ukraine’s President Volodmyr Zelenskyy slammed Trump’s diesel deal as “a gift” to Russia’s President Vladimir Putin that will help fund his war effort.

While European countries have also criticised Trump’s embrace of Russian energy, the US president has accused them of “hypocrisy”, as figures show that European Union countries continue to import Russian gas.

In his executive order on Friday, Trump called off numerous planned Russia-related sanctions days before they were due to take effect, including duties on Russian goods and penalties for buying the country’s oil and gas.

The now-blocked measures were part of legislation passed in Congress with bipartisan support last month , named after the late US Senator Lindsay Graham, an outspoken critic of Russia.

They would have included up to 100 percent tariffs on all goods brought into the US from the five top importers of Russian crude oil or gas, including China and India. They could also have imposed equal penalties on countries deemed to have knowingly bought oil or gas from Russia 30 days after the law’s implementation, or to be among the top five countries helping Moscow circumvent sanctions on sales of its oil.

The waiver will hold until the Trump administration believes “further action is appropriate”, according to the executive order.

US Congressman Don Beyer, a Democrat from Virginia, said the sanctions waiver amounts to a “surrender to Putin” that “betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent”.

Vasily Astrov, an economist at the Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Russian government will likely be the greatest beneficiary because the easing of sanctions means Russian oil will not have to be further discounted.

He estimated that about 60 cents of every extra dollar in the price of a barrel of Russian oil would “end up in state coffers”.

Russian official Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy for Putin, hailed the US decision to waive the sanctions as “an important and truly historic moment”.

Other beneficiaries include major importers of Russian oil and gas, such as China and India, who are now less exposed to the risk of secondary US penalties.

While Trump hopes the measures will also help bring down oil prices for US consumers before November mid-term elections, experts say that is less certain.

Addressing the US’s recent diesel deal with Russia, EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis said it is unlikely to have a significant impact on global prices.

According to Trump, that deal would bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel into US and global markets “immediately”, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November, and 1 million tonnes afterwards.

“If we look at the volumes, they are not of any macroeconomic significance, and frankly, there are strong doubts whether Russia is even able to supply those volumes, and according also to US quality standards, those are big question marks,” Dombrovskis told the AFP news agency.

Which countries still buy oil from Russia?

China and India are the largest buyers of Russian crude oil, purchasing 6 billion euros ($6.74bn) and 3.6 billion euros ($4.04bn) worth respectively in September, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a nonprofit think tank.

Hungary and Slovakia, the landlocked EU members that have exemptions to the bloc’s ban on Russian crude, also remain big customers, buying a combined 290 million euros ($326m) worth of the commodity in September, said CREA. Turkiye imported 172 million euros ($193m) worth of Russian crude oil the same month, the think tank added.

Since the end of 2022, the largest importers of Russian oil products, which include diesel, have been Turkiye, China, Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Singapore.

Saudi Arabia imported the most Russian oil products in September at 534 million euros ($600m), followed by Turkiye with 321 million euros ($361m), China with 304 million euros ($342m) and India with 161 million euros ($181m).

Is Europe buying increasing amounts of gas from Russia?

“The European Council regrets the United States’ decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel,” European leaders said in a joint statement adopted following a two-day European Council meeting in Brussels this week.

But despite its own near-blanket ban on Russian oil, the EU has continued to import large quantities of Russian gas, though it plans to phase out those imports next year .

Urgewald, a Germany-based group that researches coal companies, reported this week that more than 12 million tonnes of Russian Arctic LNG was transported into EU ports from January to September this year, a 9.5 percent jump from the same period last year.

In September, EU countries imported 817 million euros ($918m) of pipeline gas, and 615 million euros ($691m) of liquefied natural gas (LNG), according to CREA.

EU members France and the Netherlands were the largest LNG importers, bringing in 446 million euros ($501m) and 116 million euros ($130m) respectively, according to the think tank. France’s LNG imports represented a 103 percent increase from the previous month, it added.

France’s President Emmanuel Macron has been among the most outspoken about Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, saying on Friday that it “sends a negative message” and would have no impact on global prices.

Hungary imported the most Russian pipeline gas of any EU member by far during the month, with 414 million euros ($465m) worth. Slovakia and Bulgaria brought in 161 million euros ($181m) and 132 million euros ($148m), respectively, according to CREA data.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV to be discharged from hospital and return to Vatican after surgery to remove lung cancer
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV received blood tests and a chest X-ray at Gemelli Hospital confirming he is well enough to return to the Vatican after surgery.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV will be discharged from Gemelli Hospital in Rome on Saturday following surgery to remove a cancerous node in his lung, according to a statement from the Holy See. "Following the doctors’ assessment this morning, Pope Leo XIV will be discharged today from Gemelli Hospital, where he was hospitalized for surgery on his right lung," the statement read. "He will leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican. Tomorrow, he will lead the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment," the statement added. The pope received blood tests and a chest X-ray Saturday, both of which confirmed he is well enough to return to the Vatican, according to Vatican News. The pope will celebrate mass in a room on the 10th floor of Gemelli Hospital before returning to the Vatican, according to the Holy See press office. DR MARC SIEGEL: POPE LEO'S LUNG SURGERY PUTS MODERN MEDICINE ALONGSIDE FAITH Pope Leo underwent thoracic surgery to remove the node on Tuesday. Following the successful surgery, doctors diagnosed him with lung adenocarcinoma, a form of lung cancer. "The Pope was in the operating room approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes. The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," a statement from the Holy See press office read. RECOVERING FROM LUNG SURGERY, POPE LEO URGES PUTIN TO AGREE TO CEASEFIRE IN RUSSIAN-HELD UKRAINE CITY "Pope Leo awoke normally after surgery and, following a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the hospital’s 10th floor," Vatican News added in a statement. While recovering, Pope Leo called Russian President Vladimir Putin and urged him to call for a ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky. POPE LEO XIV SEEN FOR FIRST TIME SINCE LUNG CANCER SURGERY AMID MAJOR RECOVERY MILESTONE "During the conversation, the Holy Father expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and called for a ceasefire to allow the delivery of food and medical assistance and the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population," a statement from the Vatican read. "Finally, the Holy Father reaffirmed the Holy See’s commitment to promoting dialogue and peace," the statement added. TRUMP WISHES POPE LEO SPEEDY RECOVERY AFTER LUNG CANCER DIAGNOSIS, SPEAKS HIGHLY OF PONTIFF'S BROTHER Russia has controlled the southern Ukrainian city since May and has not allowed any humanitarian food deliveries in the city. Oleshky also has no electricity, gas or running water, and the hospital is barely functional, according to previous Fox News Digital reporting. Fox News Digital contacted the Holy See for further comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital's Brie Stimson contributed to this report.

articles.title: Protests spread across France as ‘yellow vests’ set to join
articles.summary: Demonstrations began in mid-September at schools and have expanded, tapping into wider grievances.
articles.body:
Paris, France – Saturday is a day of many unknowns. That was how the French newspaper Le Monde described it as France braced for possible nationwide demonstrations bringing together high school students, trade unions and “yellow vest” activists.

The protests began in mid-September at a high school in the Paris suburb of Creteil, where students took to the streets over dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and what they see as a deeply unequal education system.

Since then, the mobilisation has spread to thousands of “lycees”, or upper secondary schools, across the country. It is now beginning to reflect broader anxieties in a country grappling with a combination of fiscal pressures, economic stagnation and mounting social discontent.

Teachers, trade unions and university students have joined the movement.

On Saturday, some “yellow vest” activists – remnants of the participants in the grassroots cost-of-living protests that shook President Emmanuel Macron’s first term in 2018 – have also called on supporters to join the students.

“High school students are fighting for their future. Workers are fighting to earn a living from their labour. Retirees are fighting to preserve their dignity. Our paths may differ, but our concerns can converge,” Jerome Rodrigues, a prominent “yellow vest” activist, said in a video message released last week that called on people to join Saturday’s demonstrations.

Now France is waiting to see whether those calls will translate into a large, coordinated mobilisation.

Authorities have described the unrest as among the most violent in decades, saying more than 900 police have been injured since the start of the protests. But critics argued that although some demonstrators have engaged in violence, they represent a minority and the actions of a few risk overshadowing the grievances of the wider movement.

The government has also faced criticism over its response to the protests, including the detention of thousands of minors and the use of force against young demonstrators.

More than 6,700 children had been taken into police custody since mid-September, according to reports published this week.

Human rights lawyers said several teenage students have suffered warlike injuries.

Two cases have drawn particular attention: A 15-year-old lost his hand in the explosion of a stun grenade outside a school in the northern city of Lens, and a 16-year-old in western Tours lost his sight due to an injury caused by a rubber bullet.

There are fears of further clashes on Saturday.

“This is a moment of fatigue in the country,” Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu said on Thursday. “We are in an atmosphere of perma-crisis: wars, inflation and issues surrounding purchasing power.”

The government has accused the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of inflaming the protests. The party has rejected the accusation.

While France suspended the use of stun grenades for the student demonstrations, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday that he authorised police to use them in the event of what he called “urban violence”.

Nunez also said he is expecting a “fairly significant” turnout on Saturday.

Calls on social media for members of past protest movements to join the current one have been made for weeks. The website 17octobregiletjaune.net , which tracks “yellow vest” actions, listed more than 1,750 planned protest locations across the country.

The government has tried to quell student anger by scrapping plans to increase some higher education registration fees and promising to deploy 3,000 substitute teachers to high schools. This week, it set up a national online survey for pupils to hear their concerns.

But Mathieu Roger-Lacan, a French literature teacher in a disadvantaged area and author of A Language of One’s Own, a book about the growing language gap, argued that these measures fail to address the deeper problem: an education system that struggles to provide equal opportunities.

“If you have a pool that is leaking, the answer should not be to put more water into it but to work on its structure – and that costs money too,” he said.

For Roger-Lacan, the problem is not simply how much France spends on education but how it distributes those resources.

A government report published this week said that 32 percent of the French education ministry’s budget for next year will go towards funding the pensions of retired civil servants.

Students are not only complaining about deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms but also expressing a deeper anxiety about their future.

For many, a diploma no longer feels like a guarantee of stable employment or social mobility. That concern is compounded by questions about the quality of education itself amid evidence of persistent weaknesses in French students’ academic performance.

In September, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said that French 15-year-olds’ results in mathematics and reading had fallen to among their lowest levels on record.

“There is a gap between the diploma we give at the end of school, which is given to a huge part of the population, and the reality around us, which is that many of these young students have great difficulties even in writing French,” Roger-Lacan said.

The protests come at a very difficult time for the government, which is caught between demands for better-funded public services and the need to rein in France’s debt.

The government recorded a deficit of 152.5 billion euros ($171.3bn) last year, equivalent to 5.1 percent of France’s gross domestic product (GDP). By contrast, the European Union average is 3.1 percent.

Meanwhile, public debt ballooned to 115.6 percent of GDP, the third highest in the EU after Greece and Italy.

Lecornu’s proposed 2027 budget seeks to reduce the deficit through spending restraint and tax measures, including a freeze on public sector pay and limits on pension increases.

Whether the government can make those savings without deepening public anger is another question.

The debate touches a nerve in France, where the welfare state and access to public services remain central political issues.

Macron’s decision to raise the retirement age from 62 to 64 triggered months of mass demonstrations in 2023, exposing deep opposition to reforms that many saw as unfairly burdening workers.

Now as the government prepares its next budget, it faces the challenge of persuading the public that spending cuts and other savings are necessary without further eroding confidence in public institutions.

The political stakes are high. The budget bill will be debated in a deeply divided parliament as parties position themselves before the 2027 presidential election, which will mark the end of Macron’s presidency.
