articles.title: The Cignetti effect is real: Indiana football sparks an unbelievable 'revival' in Bloomington
articles.summary: From Upstairs Pub to Memorial Stadium, Bloomington is electric as Curt Cignetti's Indiana football hosts a historic top-five Ohio State showdown.
articles.body: The crowd inside the "Upstairs Pub" started to grow as the clock turned toward Friday night on the campus of Indiana, with students getting out of class and heading towards to local drinking establishments for what was going to be a wild 24 hours. Obviously, the mood has shifted around this college town thanks to the Hoosiers winning last year's CFP title, along with having a head coach in Curt Cignetti who has turned this program into a football juggernaut in just two years. COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF IS SACRIFICING ITS SOULD TO BE BECOME AN ATM FOR CONFERENCES WITH 24-TEAM EXPANSION Whether it was the apparel stores that had fans waiting in lines for their chance to purchase Indiana gear, or the restaurants that were already filling up early Friday afternoon, it's obvious that the attitude has changed around this college town that once glossed over the football season in anticipation for basketball. Later today, it will be No. 4 Ohio State visiting No. 5 Indiana in what will be the most electric atmosphere Bloomington has seen in decades. You can call it a "revival," or the Cignetti effect, but it's not hard to notice the culture change in Bloomington. "We're a football school now, and I hate to say that about the basketball program," Edward, from just outside Indianapolis noted. "We spent years praying for some type of revival of college football within this fan base, and we finally have it during one of the craziest times in sports. "A lot of schools are trying to pull off the Indiana magic of rebuilding a program in such a short time period. And those expectations are truly centered around what transpired here in Bloomington. That part is wild to me. We expect to win football games now, which is a wonderful feeling to have. So, about Indiana beating Ohio State at home The last time a Hoosiers' football team defeated the Buckeyes in Bloomington was in 1988. It took thirty years for Indiana to snap a losing streak to Ohio State, which finally came to an end last season inside Lucas Oil Stadium in the Big Ten championship game. Also, this will be the first time a top-five college football matchup has taken place inside Memorial Stadium since 1960, as Indiana rises a 22-game winning streak into their showdown with the Buckeyes on Saturday. Essentially, there are a lot of firsts that could end up coming to fruition for an Indiana team that has defied the odds over the past two seasons, against plenty of odds and fans who might still be under the impression this was all just a fluke. I'm here to tell you that nothing Curt Cignetti is doing on this campus, and opposing ones, is centered around some magical voodoo that the Hoosiers head coach has placed on the Big Ten. CURT CIGNETTI WAS SO FOCUSED THIS OFFSEASON, HE TURNED DOWN ALL EXTERNAL REQUESTS: 'I'M 95% FOOTBALL' Whether or not folks outside Bloomington believe Indiana can do it again this season is not the point. The supporters who are lining Kirkwood avenue, or the thousands who made their way into town on Friday evening, are the true barometer of where this program has been taken in such a short time period that has other college athletic directors trying to replicate the Cignetti magic. "I don't think folks truly understood what we were going through as a fan base," Thomas, longtime season ticket holder told OutKick. "I've been coming to games for thirty years, and I've never seen this type of excitement, and it's hard to correlate it with basketball. Sure, we're not oblivious to the narrative that followed our football program like a black cloud. "But, why do you think we're not taking these moments for granted? We've earned this sh-t, and I promise you this fan base isn’t cocky. We just expect to win now, which clearly wasn’t the case just a few years ago. So yea, I expect us to beat Ohio State." If Indiana can do it, so can others around college football I've been around plenty of college campuses during my career, and the resurgent joy that you see in Bloomington is contagious. This is no longer a loyal group of fans waiting for November to roll around so they can walk into Assembly Hall to watch the basketball program, which has also had its problems over the years. But what Indiana football did for the school is provide hope that everything that has transpired over the last two years in one sport, can be done again across multiple venues across campus. Curt Cignetti has not just provided a championship mindset for the passionate fans that were sitting through days of blowouts and small glimmers of hope in past years. The man who told you all to 'google' him has reignited an athletic department and fan base that will make Saturday's atmosphere on Indiana's campus feel more like a cinematic backdrop that will host college football's premier matchup of the day. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD At the same time, since it's happening here in Bloomington, there are programs across the country that now believe they can pull-off the same type magical story that we're witnessing take place with Indiana.

articles.title: CJI to visit Ladakh tomorrow to inaugurate Ladakh bench of High Court
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: The Chief Justice of India, Justice Surya Kant, will visit Ladakh on Sunday to inaugurate the newly constituted Ladakh bench of the High Court
articles.body: SRINAGAR: The Chief Justice of India, Justice Surya Kant, will visit Ladakh on Sunday to inaugurate the newly constituted Ladakh bench of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, Chief Secretary Ashish Kundra said at a press conference today.He said the CJI will be accompanied by four Supreme Court judges, the chief justice of the Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh High Court, and other high court judges. The attorney general of India will also attend the event, he said.“It is a very big thing. Frankly speaking in recent times, if you scan the history of the High Courts in India, I don't think that in the last 40 years any sitting bench has been set up in this fashion for any other High Court. The only example which comes to my mind is maybe that of the North Eastern States, where the Guwahati High Court, had benches in Arunachal Pradesh, where I have worked,” he said.“Justice coming closer to the people is a very big thing,” the CS said.“Otherwise, anyone who was aggrieved and wanted to file a writ petition would have to go to Srinagar or Jammu. I think the fact that this is now possible here in Ladakh is an extremely positive development,” he added. He said the bench was established within two months and was not among the demands raised during negotiations, describing it as a unilateral initiative by the Centre.Negotiations are currently underway between Ladakhi political leaders and the Ministry of Home Affairs. articles.title: Harry Styles debuts emotional new song dedicated to Liam Payne
articles.summary: The pop star performed the song on the second anniversary of Liam Payne's death.
articles.body:
Harry Styles performed an unreleased song he wrote for his former One Direction bandmate Liam Payne.

The Grammy Award-winning star played the track, called What Is Enough, during his sold-out concert at Madison Square Garden, on the second anniversary of Payne's death.

Styles is currently performing at the New York venue as part of a residency on his record-breaking Together, Together tour.

Addressing the packed crowd on Friday night, the singer paid tribute to Payne as a friend and someone he "wouldn't have been able to do this without".

As a spotlight shone over him, Styles made a moving speech, in which he honoured Liam Payne, who died two years ago after falling from from a hotel balcony in Argentina.

"I feel incredibly lucky to get to play these shows here in New York, and this building means a lot to me," said the artist.

"There are so many people in my life, friends and people that I've worked with that I wouldn't have been able to do this without," he continued.

"And two years ago today, I lost one of those friends."

This was met with cheers from the audience, who were hearing What Is Enough for the first time.

Wearing a royal blue jumper with a red collar, the musician then urged fans to keep an eye out for and support each other.

"I'm sure a lot of you have been through similar things. I hope you haven't.

"But really, it's just about looking after each other."

He added that there were "so many more people who have touched my life in such special ways", thanking those who helped him get to where he is.

"I'm gonna play you a song I wrote for my friend about two years ago, if that's all right."

As he paused, passionate cheers and clapping could be heard from his fans.

The singer then began to play his guitar and perform What is Enough, which featured emotional and reflective lyrics.

As he sang out to the crowd, his band played a melodic accompaniment.

Sharing their reaction to Friday night's performance on Instagram, Harry Styles' fans described What is Enough as "beautiful".

Styles launched his solo career in 2017 after becoming a global star in One Direction.

His first album and single were both UK number ones, while his record Harry's House won a Grammy and a Brit Award after its release in 2022.

articles.summary: A fingerprint on an 8-year-old's communion purse finally identified Chicago cop Thomas McInerney as Gloria Kowalewicz's killer after 65 years, police say.
articles.body: More than 65 years of searching for a killer has ended: Chicago police say they now know who shot an 8-year-old girl walking to mass. He was part of the force. Chicago cop Thomas F. McInerney Jr. has been identified as the man who abducted, shot and killed Gloria Kowalewicz on Nov. 12, 1960. FORMER CHICAGO POLICE DETECTIVE LINKED BY DNA TO 8-YEAR-OLD GIRL'S COLD-CASE MURDER, POLICE SAY At the time, McInerney was a recent addition to the agency, a violent crimes detective with the Chicago Police Department. He died in 2006. But evidence pointing to him as the killer lived on. And recent improvements in technology finally brought answers. DNA TECHNOLOGY LEADS TO ARREST IN 1988 KILLING OF ORLANDO WOMAN AFTER NEARLY FOUR DECADES Just before 8 a.m. on the morning of her death, Kowalewicz began walking a few blocks from her home to St. Mary of Mt. Carmel Church. She never arrived. About four hours later, her body was found in a ditch in a forest preserve southwest of Chicago. Her killer left evidence scattered at the scene of the crime and along a highway back to Chicago. Investigators found a bullet, Kowalewicz’s coat, her shoes, and her little, white communion purse that held her prayer book. But the killer was never identified. But recently, investigators pursued more clues using updated technology. Ultimately, it was a fingerprint lifted off the strap of her purse that led investigators to McInerney after more than six decades. DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON Rogue cop As part of the investigation, Chicago police formed a task force. They knocked on hundreds of doors and interviewed more than 1,300 people in the hopes of finding the girl's killer. More than a dozen people were questioned under a polygraph. The man responsible continued to blend inside the department. "It's not that law enforcement was incompetent at the time—they just didn't have the sophisticated investigative tools," said Michael Gould, a founding member of the New York Police Department’s K-9 unit. Using K-9 teams to track the scent of the killer could have been a more effective strategy, Gould told Fox News Digital. But using dogs to investigate crimes wasn’t widely adopted until the mid ‘80s, Gould said. Now, they’re routinely used and have "cracked a lot of missing person cases." "Dogs could have tracked where the person lived and what direction he fled." "They give us X-ray vision. They allow us to see things—evidence—that's invisible to the naked eye. And that's what the primary locating tool should be for law enforcement, police K-9." KILLER EX-COP EXECUTED FOR CHILD'S SLAYING AS SHERIFF SAYS HE’S SURE SAME MONSTER MURDERED ANOTHER GIRL Chicago Police Department detectives never stopped searching for the girl’s killer, according to a statement sent by the agency to Fox News Digital. Through the years, they worked with Illinois State Police and the FBI to continue a quest for answers. The DNA and fingerprint evidence was preserved for decades until, finally, technology advanced enough to bring answers. "My prediction there are going to be other victims [linked to McInerney]. I don't think this was a sole act." articles.title: BROADCAST BIAS: Feminist freakout over Shane Gillis comment is the real joke
articles.summary: NBC's "Saturday Night Live" faced a media firestorm after Shane Gillis joked about women's gym clothes, drawing accusations of misogyny and, even rape culture.
articles.body: In recent years, NBC’s "Saturday Night Live" has followed the late-night trend of waging a self-righteous "humor" war on President Donald Trump. Almost every show begins with a Trump-mocking skit, and the "Weekend Update" fake newscast is heavily laden with snide comments about Trump and his conservative coterie. What caused thumping outrage this week was comedian Shane Gillis, who was announced as an incoming "SNL" cast member in 2019 before getting canceled almost immediately for some anti-Asian jokes. His opening monologue this week was denounced for joking, "I haven’t been to the gym in so long. I didn’t know women just dress like whores now. Look, I'm sorry, there's no other way to describe. Have you seen it? I've seen it, the shorts. Have you seen the shorts? Those neon, they’re, like, artificial vape-colored. The wrinkles go, like, around the cheeks and combine at the butthole." What drew less attention was the second half of it, Gillis mocking himself, or men in general: "And don’t look. You’re not allowed to look. For real, don’t look, because they are filming. I’m in the background of like 10 TikToks right now." ACTOR DAN LEVY BLASTS SHANE GILLIS' 'SNL' MONOLOGUE, CLAIMS MEN'S 'COMPLACENCY' FUELS SEXUAL ASSAULT The first broadcast network to pounce on Gillis was actually NBC, on NBCNews.com. Reporter Rebecca Cohen lamented: "Gillis, who is known for his raunchy style of comedy, has a history of placing women — and other marginalized groups — at the butt of jokes. Many people called it tone-deaf of Gillis to make such comments following the reports around a former Cornell University student who alleged she was gang-raped at an on-campus fraternity house in 2024." "Many people" were represented by feminist author Jessica Valenti: "This is his contribution to that conversation," she said. "This is him telling us what he thinks of the discourse on sexual assault. ... That is rape culture." SALLY YATES' CORNELL REVIEW OF ALLEGED GANG RAPE COULD SCRUTINIZE CRUCIAL POLICE INTERVIEW, ATTORNEY SAYS NBC’s "Today" picked it up on air on Tuesday in the fourth hour. "I wouldn’t want my kids to listen to that," co-host Jenna Bush Hager said. "It feels mean," co-host Sheinelle Jones agreed. "And that is the energy that I think made people upset." "Today" also put the controversy on TV when fake "Weekend Update" anchor Michael Che came on to promote his new Netflix special. "How are you thinking about what happened this week with Shane’s opening monologue?" substitute host Laura Jarrett asked. "You’ve seen the pushback." SWIFTIES CLAIM TRAVIS KELCE DID THE UNSPEAKABLE BY LIKING SHANE GILLIS' 'SNL' MONOLOGUE & THEY'RE NOT HAPPY Che replied: "That’s comedy. It’s like, you think it’s funny and then some people don’t." Jarrett asked Che if he laughed in real time. He denied seeing it in real time, as he prepared for his skit. Che also did an interview on NPR’s "Morning Edition," but they never brought Gillis up. NPR White House correspondent Danielle Kurtzleben posted an angry thread on Bluesky: "I know this is nothing you haven’t heard before but like In the year of our Lord 2026 a dude went on the big comedy sketch institution program and said 'lol women dress like whores' and … it’s all fine and good? It’s not all over my feeds? Is it bc no one watches SNL or like I dunno normal misogyny?" Profanity followed. CORNELL PROTESTERS SWARM CAMPUS TO SUPPORT JANE DOE, CALL FOR UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT'S RESIGNATION On ABC’s "The View," co-host Sara Haines picked up the "rape culture" spin: "When the language like ‘whore’ is passed along, I might have not noticed it before in the past, because it was under the guise of a joke. And as we’re talking about this Cornell 7, I'm not saying a joke makes an assault, but it makes it much easier to look at it as another human as an object." It wasn’t misogyny, apparently, on ABC’s "Jimmy Kimmel Live," when the host displayed a picture of then-White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia in skin-tight gym clothes to make fun of how unqualified she was: "Katie met a number of qualifications for the job. She has blonde hair. She can do a thumbs up, and end of list. Really, what else do you need? Where do they all get that same face? Is that makeup, or do they have a machine that stamps it on?" Che replied: "That’s comedy. It’s like, you think it’s funny and then some people don’t." SETH MEYERS, JOHN OLIVER TELL JIMMY KIMMEL HE'S THEIR 'BULLETPROOF VEST' WHEN IT COMES TO TRUMP By the time the Gillis controversy was picked up on "CBS Mornings" on Oct. 14, there was at least a debate of sorts. Co-host Nate Burleson set it up: "The question is: Is he being targeted unfairly by cancel culture, or does he deserve all of this criticism he’s getting?" After running through outraged clips, co-host Adriana Diaz admitted Gillis "recently broke a Guinness World Record for the largest attendance ever at a comedy show with nearly 74,000 audience members." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION But they kept up the anti-women angle: "Sophie Carpenter is a fitness coach and content creator. She worries jokes like the one Gillis made Saturday could discourage some women from working out altogether." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP All this fuss might cause the sneaking suspicion that NBC wanted its comedy "institution" to make news, which would explain why they were the first ones out of the gate in denouncing it. It’s likely this will only help Gillis, just as he built his career on getting canceled by NBC in the first place.
